chapters.title: Chapter Six
paragraphs: January 22, 2022

It was Saturday, and Anton and I were celebrating our anniversary. Early in the morning, he showed up with a huge bouquet. It contained an odd number of red roses. I always got those from him. Suddenly, I even forgot how many years we had been together. In theory, one could have calculated it from the bouquet, but in eternity, a year here or there doesn't matter.

He brought the flowers straight to my bed. I don't know when he went to get them, because I don't think a single florist is open before eight, though with the amount of flowers he's bought me, I wouldn't have been surprised if they had been at his disposal with personalized opening hours.

Before we lived together, he had it easier. Toward evening, he'd pick me up and take me out for dinner. Now he had to spend the whole day with me, and on special occasions, I liked to feel special. Not that he ever seemed to mind. He might even have enjoyed planning the programs.
"Today we're going to do something a little different than usual," he said.
"What do you mean?" I asked. "Aren't we going to a restaurant?"
"Of course we are."
"Then it will be pretty much the same as usual."
"No, because before that, we're going somewhere you don't really like."
"Hmm, you're daring, I like it! But you know that when I'm disappointed, I'm not very good company."
"You are always excellent company," he fibbed. "Though you might end up disappointed."
"Where are we going?"
"To the thermal baths."
"Right. I'm not a big fan," I replied.
"It will be special."
"What makes you say that?"
"Because it's the most beautiful bathhouse in the city, and they finished the renovation just a few weeks ago. It's become quite a trendy place lately."
"I sound quite shallow when you put it like that. But the truth is, I actually like it better for that very reason."

It wouldn't have mattered where we went today, because what I really wanted was to be able to think through, with a clear head, the wealth of information we had managed to acquire in recent days. Matt and Wilbur were still working through Jess's list, and I was trying to organize my thoughts. In the meantime, Jessica went back to the countryside. I arranged police protection for her, and in theory, they were doing their job completely invisibly. This could have worried me, but the captain reassured me that they worked excellently and would notice everything possible. I had to believe what he said; I had no other choice anyway.

My main problem with the thermal baths was that I didn't like crowds and the thought of sharing the water with so many strangers. Of course, it was still much better than going to some dirty lake, though on January 22, that obviously wasn't an option. I hoped there would at least be some secluded spot in the baths where we could talk a little more intimately.

It usually helped a lot if I could talk through the things swirling in my head with Anton. He asked good questions about cases and could think logically, which, let's face it, was to be expected of him after writing so many crime novels.

After the renovation, small cabins were created where two people could comfortably retreat from the crowd, and in the pool, massage jets helped those wishing to rest to relax. It took us a long time to snag one, but afterward, we wouldn't have given it up for anything, no matter how much the pushy people tried to make a nuisance of themselves.
"You said you'd tell me this weekend what you've come up with so far," Anton noted, while I lay cradled in his arms in the shallow water.
"Yes, I wanted to wait a bit for it to settle," I replied. "There's quite a lot of things I need answers to."
"Tell me!" he encouraged, kissing my neck.
"I don't even know where to begin. I thought a lot about whether to tell you."
"Oh dear!" he chimed in.
"You'll see in a moment. I wasn't tense for no reason these past few days."
"I didn't even notice."
"Right, of course," I replied. "Jess was threatened."
"Already?" Anton was puzzled.
"Does that seriously surprise you?"
"Don't tell me you didn't expect it. How did it get out so soon?"
"That's the one thing I don't have the answer to."
"How did it happen?"
"A note was left in her mailbox."
"Doesn't sound very serious."
"Except for what it said. That she dies if she doesn't withdraw the complaint."
"Then let her withdraw it," Anton declared.
"Of course."
"Why? It's completely logical."
"We worked on this for years! You're saying we should just leave it at that?"
"No," he answered briefly.
"Then I don't understand you."
"I'm just saying you should withdraw the complaint. You can still keep investigating."
"Yes, but that won't lead to a trial."
"If there's enough evidence, the state will prosecute instead of Jess," he said, as if it were the most obvious thing. What really hurt was that it actually was.
"Yes, that does seem like a viable option."
"Should I solve another of your problems?" he asked contentedly.
"You haven't solved this one yet, but it's a good start," I replied. "I have to discuss it with Jess to see what she says. She wanted to go through with this, no matter what."
"I can understand that. But in this situation, it's better to be cautious."
"I have a cop assigned to her. In theory, they'll watch her every step."
"Every day?"
"Yes."
"I mean, a cop every single moment of every day?"
"Obviously, several people will perform the task."
"I don't trust that kind of thing," he said, unwittingly feeding my anxiety.
"Aren't you supposed to be helping me relax?" I asked.
"Of course. You're the professional; I only know how things work in books."
"And you wouldn't trust them there?"
"In novels, the police are usually left out of the investigation."
"Of course, because it would be too simple if they solved the case right away."
"Yes, that's probably what's behind it."
"So then? Why is it a bad idea?"
"It's not that it's bad. I just said I don't trust this solution, but that's not the police's fault. Between the two of us, you're the rational one, and this really is your territory."
"Okay, but you've put a bug in my ear, so it would be better if we changed the subject."
"What else is there?" Anton asked.
"That depends on what you want to hear about."
"About everything."
"Fine, fine, obviously. But one step at a time."
"How did Jess handle the questioning?" he asked.
"At first she was nervous, but then she got into it," I replied. "By the end, she spoke quite convincingly."
"When you're telling the truth, it's not that hard to be convincing. Did she tell you everything?"
"More or less. Obviously not everything. A little less than what I'd suggested."
"What didn't she talk about?"
"How she shut down the Neon Nights."
"That was pretty hardcore."
"Yeah. It must have been awesome. Too bad I didn't see it... How are you?" I changed the subject, because Anton finally noticed that I had been longingly caressing his thigh for minutes.
"I think you know exactly," he smiled.
"I see!" I teased, and continued. "Well, yes. As it happens, this place could be quite exciting."
"Quite exciting indeed."
"I wonder if it's the people or the pool that makes it so," I mused.
"Mostly you."
"Right. That's the correct answer," I added, and kissed him.

These private spots weren't very deep. You could easily be seen even if you were just lying down, so it took some courage to want to get more out of the situation. But then, it was our anniversary. It was obvious that we both wanted to spice up the day with a little adventure, finding a perfect balance between risk and reward.

I slid my hand slightly higher up Anton's thigh, so that through the leg of his swim trunks, I could reach all the way to his backside. I tried to cover this movement with my leg, drawing my thigh close to the hem of his trunks. This allowed him to reach me too, and looking into each other's eyes with loving gazes, we began to please each other.

The water indeed proved to be very shallow. At first, I touched Anton in the usual way, but it soon became clear that doing so would immediately expose a quite unmistakable shape through his trunks, which wouldn't have been easy to hide. Since we tried to remain in the most natural position possible so that anyone looking at us would think we were just resting, I turned his hard, swelling member toward the leg of his trunks and began to move it gently back and forth. We didn't want to start wild lovemaking—that would have been too much—but we didn't want to let this special occasion go to waste either.

Anton also touched me very gently. First he touched my thigh; he took his time. In the water, everything felt completely different anyway. Touches didn't glide as easily, and it took him longer to find the entrance. He caressed and circled persistently, which filled me with a very pleasant feeling even before he got further in. I felt wonderful. I tried to relax as much as possible and focus only on the slow, fine movements, which seemed to switch on another sense in me. We didn't rush; we proceeded patiently on the path to pleasure, paying much more attention to each other than at other times when we are suddenly carried away by longing. We didn't speak. We lay on each other with closed eyes, imagining connected neural pathways in my mind, almost seeing how the stimulus triggered the impulse. How different it is this way, I thought. How many sexual encounters I had experienced in my life, and yet for years, there wasn't a single one that was even remotely comparable to the most cliché, boring occasion among those I experienced with Anton.

I knew how to handle him; I'd proved this to Anton quite a few times. Sometimes he couldn't resist my touch for even a minute. Not even when I was barely doing anything. This time too, I was on the right path. I could tell by his breathing which step of the ladder I was on, but I didn't want him to finish yet, so I returned to caressing his thigh. He did just the opposite. I didn't mind, because I loved feeling good, and between the two of us, he was demonstrably the more impatient one. If I withheld something from him, he wanted to make up for it by pleasing me, pushing his fingers deeper inside me than before. I didn't really want to control my reactions. We behaved completely normally—or at least, that's what I told myself—and the heavy breathing that escaped me could easily have been mistaken for signs of sleepy relaxation.

When I gripped Anton again, he didn't say it, but I could tell he didn't want to be left hanging; he was aching for fulfillment. I tried to please him, especially since he had really outdone himself in the last few minutes and didn't deserve to be kept waiting even a second. So I began to move my hand more firmly, caressing his entire length. I hadn't planned exactly where he would ejaculate, because I hadn't cared about that detail at all. In the shallow water, there was a drain where the current swirled more strongly, so when we reached the end, I tried to guide the white fluid there. We both handled it in a civilized manner. Anton's smile revealed everything, and when he opened his eyes, he saw me batting my eyelashes to let him know how crazy I still was about him after all these years.
We lay on each other for a few minutes. It was a very reassuring feeling. Then, as if another self had gotten the upper hand, we returned to the open questions.
"And what else is there?" he inquired.
"A man set on fire."
"A what now?"
"His name was Mike Alioglu. He wanted to get into the Neon Nights."
"Chilling," Anton noted. Such things always upset him.
"I don't really want to think about it either. I have no idea what he did, but I'm sure he didn't deserve such a death."
"And how do you know this happened?"
"From a statement."
"Whose?"
"I don't know yet. The name was redacted in the statement. They probably didn't want to get them into trouble."
"So later investigators wouldn't find them..."
"That would make sense, but they were eventually cleared in the investigation files. They didn't kill Mike. In theory, they were friends."
"It would be good to ask them about it directly," Anton suggested.
"Believe it or not, that occurred to me too, but we have to find them first."
"Maybe Mike's relatives knew them."
"Sometimes the most obvious things are right in front of us. You're right. Mike's relatives must know them."
"How exciting! You should talk to them as soon as possible."
"Look how excited you got," I laughed. "I'll find out who the witness was, and once we find them, we'll talk to them."
"We'll talk? Meaning, you and me?" his eyes lit up.
"The detectives and me. Yes."
He looked slightly disappointed by that answer.
"The water has cooled down, let's go!" he suggested suddenly.
Since I felt the same way, I didn't object. But by the changing cabins, Anton started up again.
"Amy, wait! Was the note threatening Jess handwritten?"
"Yes," I replied, then thought about it. "Are you thinking that...?"
"You can learn a lot from even a single sentence."
"But we have nothing to compare it to. We don't know who wrote it."
"We don't need to. It can still help narrow down the suspects. Ask Jess for the note."
"I don't know, Anton. We're looking for a complete stranger."
"And what if they're not?"
"What do you mean?"
"Maybe they're not."
"Maybe we know them from the past, but even if we found out who wrote it, what would it matter? We know it's one of Mortenstein's people."
"Yes. That's for sure."
"So? What's your point with this?" I asked.
"I don't know, Amy. It just occurred to me."
"I'll ask her to send it, then you can look into it."
"Great!" A smile spread across Anton's face.
"Do you really enjoy this that much?"
"Yes, I need a bit more action," he said, winking.
"Meaning...?"

With that, he grabbed me and practically pushed me into the nearest changing cabin.
"We just finished..." I began, though I didn't even know why I said it.
"Don't you want to?" he whispered in my ear, already pulling my swimsuit down.
"Sure, that's why you've already got your trunks off," I retorted, and my hand was indeed doing something completely different from what my words would have suggested.
In an instant, I jumped into his lap, and we began kissing wildly. He entered me immediately, which surprised me since I couldn't understand how he had gotten hard again so quickly.

I was surprised by his sudden intensity, which only turned me on more. He went very deep inside me; unlike before, our animal instincts took over completely. Anton didn't hesitate; he fell upon me immediately from behind, grabbing my breasts tightly, making it even more intense. chapters.title: Chapter Seven
paragraphs: January 25, 2022

Three days had already passed since Anton tried to convince me to withdraw the complaint. I completely understood why he argued for this; to tell the truth, I didn't take the threat lightly either, but I also knew that the first time they only wanted to scare Jess. However, Jessica wouldn't hear of it. No matter how much I explained to her that the investigation could still continue, she didn't want to accept it. She said she would look weak, and that they only wanted to make her feel vulnerable. In this, let's face it, she was entirely right. She knew them well; she knew exactly how they function and what methods they work with.

So my persuasion did not succeed. The police continued their supervision of Jessica and her partner, sending summaries every day. From these, it was evident that they indeed paid attention to every detail, as well as the fact that so far nothing noteworthy had happened in Montaukville. This didn't surprise me. I didn't expect anyone to hover around Jess's home daily, nor to do so conspicuously. The police's task was primarily to thwart the threat's content; the observation of the protected individuals belonged to the protection only subsidiarily. Thus, from the perspective of the investigation, we didn't gain extra information.

At my request, Jess sent a photo of the note containing the threat, with which Anton set to work immediately to find out more about its writer. He called the writers' union, from where he got the contact info of a recognized graphologist; because of this, he had high hopes for the analysis. I could have looked for a suitable expert myself, but I promised him he could investigate this lead, so I didn't want to interfere in his work.

He was right that we must contact Mike Alioglu's relatives, but this was no easy task. Quite a few Alioglus lived in the city, and the investigation files did not contain the relatives' contact details.
Then Wilbur suddenly walked into my office in an unexpected moment.
"We have several people from the list."
"Fantastic!" I got excited. "Nice work, Wilbur. Who are they?"
"One of them is a man. His name is David King. The other is a certain Hermione."
"Hermione?" I asked back. "Like the witch girl from Harry Potter?"
"I don't know where she got her name, but that's what they call her."
"And what's her last name?"
"She has no last name, Miss Evans. It might be a stage name."
"I fear she's still working. Is there anyone else?"
"Yes, there is. Jake Cooper. The guy who recruited Jessica Marsh and her friend."

I froze completely. The mention of the boy's name who recruited us into the network was like a small electric shock. I hadn't expected at all that we could find Jake Cooper, yet now his address lay before me. I almost regretted that Jessica couldn't come with me to see him. I was sure she could have squeezed much more out of him than I could. But that was why I had detectives, so I wouldn't have to be the tough one. If one had to ask nicely, keeping to all legal norms, Amanda Evans was perfectly suited; but if someone felt like being stubborn, they could talk to Wilbur or Matt, who only seemed like a charmingly cheerful gentleman until the end of their first sentence.
"When could you visit them?" I inquired.
"Today already, if you like."
"Of course I would, Wilbur. Let's just discuss which address belongs to whom. We should all three go to Jake Cooper. He seems the most interesting among them."
"Choose from the other two then," the bear suggested.
"You go to Hermione, and I'll visit David King."
"Won't you be in trouble alone, Miss Evans?"
"I can take care of myself," I replied, pointing toward my service weapon. "Wilbur, would you find out something else for me?"
"What would you like, Miss Evans?"
"Get the address of the Alioglu family from somewhere. You know, the family whose son was set on fire."
"All right," he answered, closing the door.

I didn't remember David King or Hermione from the times I was there. I would have been surprised if Jessica had only given me a list of people who ended up at Neon Nights after I was taken away. I remembered the faces of all the gentlemen who worked there at the time, but I couldn't remember any of them by the name of David King. He must have changed his identity too, I thought. It wouldn't surprise me, most of us did.

Poor little Alice. How scared she was when she got into the Neon Nights. How many terrible mistakes she made. How much she held herself as nothing. I couldn't blame her. She couldn't do otherwise than pile mistake upon mistake. She had no idea how she should take up the fight with life and acted completely instinctively. A few years later, however, she was no longer alive. She ceased to exist. She stopped being Alice forever. Alice, who in her surname didn't even know whose genes she was carrying forward. Alice Bucks died prematurely. But as the years passed, from Alice's ashes, Amanda Evans was born—the woman who was ready to whitewash Alice's memory.

David King lived in a narrow street that had advanced into a public space from a row of alleys forming at the back of several old tenement houses; yet it didn't exude the bad vibe that such places usually do in movies. God only knows how any vegetation settled in this dark place; from wherever the sun shone, it was always in shadow. Anyone visiting here for the first time would know they wouldn't meet wealthy people. It was depressing to see this, since the gentlemen earned plenty of money to easily buy apartments even in the city's prestigious districts.

David King's name was on the intercom, which meant he didn't rent the apartment he lived in. At least he managed that much in life, I thought. I dreaded the meeting, even though I had never known him. I recoiled from talking to a person who was part of the exploitation of the girls, even if, as it seemed, all he got out of it was to buy an apartment in this pathetic neighborhood. I couldn't feel sorry for him. He could have lost much more, and even that wouldn't have been enough.

Many of us became drug addicts because they couldn't stand wanting to throw up every morning, so much did they disgust themselves with whom they saw in the mirror. However, this wasn't only the case for the girls. Some gentlemen also couldn't process what they did day in and day out. David King must have been among them.
A thin man's voice spoke in the intercom. He let me in.

The apartment was on the third floor. In the stairwell and the hallway, the plaster was peeling, while the walls exuded a slight smell of damp. Knowing myself, I would have committed suicide if I had had to live here. To my surprise, however, a polite stranger greeted me. He came out into the hallway to make sure I found my way.
"Thank you!" I greeted him, trying to remain firm.
"Come in! Forgive me, but I didn't catch your name well on the intercom," he said. "It static crackles so much, you can hear almost nothing."
"I'm Amanda Evans. Prosecutor," I continued the introduction.
"Prosecutor?" King was surprised. "Prosecutors don't visit my apartment very often. In fact, you're the first."
Unlike his apartment, there was nothing strange in this. It took me a while to realize what made the room look that way. The whole place was full of colorful accessories and clothing items.
"Please, have a seat!" he then pointed to the sofa on the side of the room.
"Very kind."
"Can I get you something?" he inquired. "A hot tea?"
"No, thank you."
It was quite chilly in those days, and a cup would have felt good, but I wouldn't have drunk uncertain drinks in a strange place even if I had been completely frozen.
"Do you live here alone?" I asked.
"Yes," he replied. "Are you asking because of the skirts?" he tried to guess the real reason for my question, since in half of the room, quite a few skirts indeed lay scattered.
"Actually, yes," I answered, slightly embarrassed.
"Those are mine," he smiled. "But I don't go out on the street in them," he excused himself.
"Oh, I just..." I would have begun to explain when he instead started.
"Those are costumes. I'm a performing artist. Though not a very successful one. I perform in several places, at the Molière Rouge, for instance. I perform in drag shows."
"Wow," escaped my surprise, though I had seen enough similar things at the Neon Nights back then. "And how long have you worked there?"
"Well, there is no such thing as there. Always elsewhere. Of course, I perform in one place multiple times, like the Molière Rouge, but I don't have one specific place."
"When did you start?"
"I wish I could say recently," he replied. "But surely ten years ago. Is this why you came?" I failed to detect any fear in his voice.
"No, not exactly. But I came because of you, obviously."
"Because of me?" he was surprised. "I'm not aware of any proceedings against me."
"There aren't any," I replied. "I'd like to hear you as a witness."
"As a witness?" he was puzzled. "But what was I a witness to?"
"I'd be interested in a club where you supposedly worked. The Neon Nights."
"Aha, that one," his tone dropped suddenly. I felt disappointment in his voice.
"My information is correct, isn't it?"
"Yes, of course. That's why I fell silent."
"Do you have such a bad opinion of the place?" I played ignorant.
"Opinion?" he asked back. "No, it's not my opinion that is bad. I don't have an opinion of it."
"Then what?"
"Phew," he sighed. "I just woke up, I didn't think I'd have to answer such a question today... I don't know. I have feelings. Mostly painful feelings."
"Why?" I tried to probe, but David King seemed to only now begin to realize what an unusual situation he was in. He decided he wanted to restart the conversation instead.
"What did you say your name was?"
"Amanda Evans," I repeated my name again, this time without my profession.
"How did you get my apartment address?"
"As I said, I'm a prosecutor. My detectives tracked it down."
"I see," King answered shortly. "Then how did you find out about me?"
"You see, that is a question deserving a very different answer."
"I'm really glad of that," he replied. "Because I'd like to know."
"From Jessica Marsh."
David King pulled his lips into a smile.
"Then you are on the good side too?" he asked, almost whispering.
"That depends on how you look at it. But what do you mean by being on the good side?"
"Jessica Marsh was a special girl. So if you are her person too, then yes, you are on the good side."
"I see what you mean. Then my answer will reassure you. She specifically asked me to visit you."
"But why?"
"She said you could help her."
"Me help her? Is she in trouble?"
"No," I replied shortly. "You can help by telling us everything."
"That will take quite a lot of time," he answered.
"Then only what I ask. What did you do at the Neon Nights?"
"At first, what everyone else did. I was a paid sex worker."
"Paid?" I was surprised by his answer.
"Yes, paid."
"Jessica Marsh claimed that the girls were worked almost as slaves."
"Sure, that was true. The girls didn't get paid. But we did."
"Who is we?"
"The men who did the same work as the girls."
"But why?" I was outraged, but soon realized that Amanda Evans had no reason to be outraged by something a former sex worker was telling her.
"I can't tell you, but that's how it was. Regardless, I think that I and those like me were at the very bottom of the ladder."
"At the very bottom? With pay in your pockets?" I threw back at him. What he said hurt.
"Yes. But a man in that environment usually had a harder time." I really couldn't listen to what he said with a straight face. My outrage was written all over my face.

"Don't get me wrong," he interrupted himself. "The question of money was only one of many. But no matter how vulnerable the girls were in the Neon Nights, they still received more protection than we did. We had no leader to look after us. We belonged to the club, but we did the most pitiful work. We had no say in the shaping of our own fate. The girls' leaders behind the scenes tried to fight for the best opportunities for their own. We, however, had no choice at all if a group of clients arrived who wanted our company. There were few of us boys."
"I see," I seemingly accepted his answer, much as I would have liked to detail at length the things in which I had no say either.

Then I realized that this man did the same work as I. He was not in a single bit better position, and I didn't even know how he would have had the chance to spend his money, because even visiting malls on a weekly basis in the company of my gentleman, I wouldn't have been able to buy even a pack of gum without him. And he, according to this, couldn't go out. There was no one to go with. It was useless to debate which of us was in a more hopeless position. If he really worked as a prostitute, he deserved this little apartment; I didn't begrudge him it.
"You couldn't go out?" I inquired.
"As I said, there were few of us. There was no day off at the club. I worked through those years without a rest day. Except if I got sick. But there was hardly an example of that."
"Mettől meddig dolgozott ott?" (How long did you work there?)
"For six years?" I disbelieved, especially since I should have known him.
"Almost six, yes."

I was surprised. I couldn't place David King's face. It wasn't familiar. I could have blamed it on it happening long ago, but that would have been no excuse. I thought I'd recognize everyone from those times. King, according to this, was an exception.
"Forgive me," he continued. "I don't want to intrude, and it might seem like a cliché, but don't we know each other? You seem familiar."
"I'm sorry, but I don't think so," I denied, though I wasn't lying to him either; I really didn't remember him. "I'm quite introverted, I don't really go out."
"Just a feeling," he replied, "it doesn't matter."
"You said you only worked as a prostitute at first. Later what was your job, did you become a supervisor?"
"Gentleman? No way! Nobody became a gentleman who came from the bottom. There was a separate procedure for that."
"Then?"
"Look around. What do you think? I gave drag performances."

Then it suddenly clicked who he was. I recalled how once on stage he gave a truly captivating performance from La Cage aux Folles. His face did look similar. Back then, however, he was about thirty kilos thinner, completely fragile, not muscular like now.
"Was that all your job?"
"Not only. My previous job description naturally remained. But a show of my own was definitely considered an advancement. And I liked doing those. It helped me survive."
"How would you describe your six years spent at the Neon Nights?"
"You really don't stop with the hard questions, do you?"
"Due to the case, unfortunately, I can't stop," I excused myself, though I didn't consider it such a hard question.
"It's not important how I experienced it. You see, to this day, I deal with what I learned there."
"Then what is important?" I inquired.

"That not everyone was as lucky as I. Three of my companions disappeared; to this day I know nothing about them. They left the club before it closed. Countless girls were ruined. Many were taken, passed on. How could this happen?"
"Look, because of the investigation, I can't say anything for now. But how do you feel, would you be willing to report on your experiences there in court?"

"I have to think about that," King answered. "Although the Neon Nights officially ceased to exist, the organization certainly remained. Besides, I don't know if you know who directed the whole thing."
"Do you mean the president?"

"I mean the president. Obviously Jessica didn't keep it a secret." He compressed his thin lips and thought for a moment. "So you too can understand if I weigh what I can win or lose with such a testimony."
"Of course I understand. But we're going to need witnesses. Do you know anyone else who could testify?"
"To tell the truth, no. I haven't bumped into anyone since I got away from there. I didn't want to, either. I bought this apartment with my saved money and tried to do my thing quietly."

"Then I hope you'll say yes in the end," I answered. I didn't even want to hear that he wanted to protect even this insignificant existence of his. "If something should occur to you, you can call me at this number anytime. Anytime." I emphasized the flexibility of my availability, while handing a business card to David King.
"It's okay," he answered. "Maybe I'll call you. Maybe I'll confess, maybe not," he answered uncertainly.
"Contact me!" I turned back from the door. "There are few people who can come into play. You are needed."
"Goodbye!" he said, closing the door.

chapters.title: Chapter Eight
paragraphs: So David King was no gentleman. He was a simple sex worker who later turned to drag shows. I couldn't quite take in what he said. My thoughts were interrupted by the honking of cars. Hurrying people scrambled to catch their buses. It was foggy and it looked like spray was falling from the sky. My coat was slowly soaking wet as I cursed myself for not grabbing the umbrella by the door in the morning. I headed for the subway. And my thoughts revolved around the case again.

I didn't understand why he was glad that I was on the good side if he didn't want to help. In fact, how foolish it sounds: the good side. We weren't divided into camps of good and bad. None of us was sinless. At least I didn't feel that way, and as far as I knew, neither did Jessica. We were victims, but not sinless. In reality, there was no good side on which we could stand. When did we become guilty? Who knows. But someone who is good doesn't decide to sell themselves out and start stripteasing. We weren't good, but we didn't know what it meant to be, either. We were obedient for a long time, and although they labeled us as good in return, we knew this wasn't true. For someone who is good, a man's genitals don't end up in her mouth at the age of nine, or anywhere else.
Jess and I learned early that being a "good girl" actually meant bad, because real good girls didn't do what the "good girls" did. Not even, perhaps, if they had no other choice.

Regardless, I hoped for David King's testimony. His story was authentic. It would have looked really good in a trial, especially when he spoke of his ruined acquaintances. But then he realized he was afraid, realized he was over it, and already had something to lose. I was angry at him for that. Jess's presence might convince him, I thought. She hadn't given his name for nothing.

We planned to go to the address belonging to Jake Cooper with the detectives in the afternoon. I didn't know how things were going with Hermione, but I thought they could get important information. I didn't know Hermione, though after my meeting with David King I was no longer so sure of that. At any rate, I didn't remember her under such a name.

What was I expecting? Unlike other investigations, I no longer had to convince myself that the accused was indeed guilty. Skipping past that, I already had to work on gathering the evidence. You might think the two are the same, but somehow they aren't. Every time I started an investigation, there was always a moment when I felt I already believed the person was guilty. Until that happened, however, I focused much more on convincing myself. I was interested not only in legally valid evidence, but in everything that could strengthen suspicion and thereby convince me.

Is it bias to believe someone is guilty without proper evidence? Perhaps. But I couldn't work any other way. I didn't dispense the truth. My job was to search out all evidence that could support the charge. I just wanted to get closer to the truth.

Now, however, I didn't have to convince myself. From the start, I had to look at the case through a completely different lens. If I didn't feel something could serve as evidence, I didn't bother with it. David King's story was interesting, but he said nothing that fundamentally reshaped my image of Neon Nights. It didn't help me. But it could have helped the court if he honestly recounted how he experienced his years spent there.

I approached Hermione the same way. If she wants to talk, and knows what to talk about, that's great. If, on the other hand, she doesn't want to stand before the general public, I won't be able to use her for anything, just as if she didn't exist.

Precisely because of this, I had to trust Jessica that she had given good names. There was a reason why I couldn't list them myself. All my hope lay in Jessica to connect me with those who could meaningfully advance our case. Unfortunately, there weren't many, as I also told David King.

I definitely wanted to have lunch before the meeting. It was past noon by the time my train pulled into François Étudiant Square. There was a bistro near the prosecutor's office, where I always found something I liked from the daily menu. To my surprise, Anton called me for the exact same reason.
"I'm almost there," I replied.
"Five minutes for me, but then your jaw is going to drop."

Anton knew how to exaggerate. As a writer, I felt he sometimes saw the world in more colorful tones than it actually was. My jaw hadn't dropped from anything in a very long time, and I didn't think anything was about to happen that would change that.
I ordered two chicken dishes; we both liked it, and at least I knew what we were getting. When he arrived, he sat opposite me with almost stormy speed.
"You won't believe this," he began.
"I can't wait to doubt it. I haven't ordered a drink yet, what should I get you?"
"The graphologist said that Jessica must know the person who wrote the threat."
"Interesting..."
"You don't believe him?"

"It doesn't really matter what I believe, Anton," I said somewhat bluntly—I didn't want to offend him, but I was hungry. "The question is whether we can use it for anything. For now, I don't see how, for several reasons. Let's assume Jess really knows who wrote this. Would that surprise us? Not really, since she knew everyone at Neon Nights."
"But it's still strange that a woman wrote it."
"A woman?" I asked. "That indeed makes the whole thing more interesting."
"What kind of day did you have?" he inquired.
"The witness, I'm afraid, won't play ball," and then I told him about my conversation with David King.
"You really didn't remember him?" he asked.
"Why, did you?"
"It was the first drag show I ever saw."
"And how do you think I should convince him?"
"You don't have to convince him," he replied. "Jess will. Just give her time." Vivacity shone in his blue eyes, and once he felt he had reassured me, he waved to a server.
"Two lemonades, please," I finally said to the waiter.

chapters.title: Chapter Nine
paragraphs: We met Matt and Wilbur at 2:45 PM in the parking lot in front of the prosecutor's office. When I inquired on the phone about what they had learned from Hermione, they admitted, somewhat uncomfortably, that not much, because she refused to speak with them. It did turn out, however, that Hermione is blind.

I only knew one girl who was blind in the Neon Nights, and she hadn't been blind when she arrived. She lost her sight as a result of an accident, or to be completely honest, a client beat her in the face with a champagne bottle so badly that her optic nerve was damaged. Her name was Mary Morales. She was a very beautiful Latina girl; many adored her. Even after the incident, her popularity did not wane. She kept working just the same. Maybe it even helped her that she could no longer see who she was with. It would have helped me, but they never allowed the lights to be turned off when we were with a client.

I was inclined to believe that Mary Morales was Hermione, and had been living under a stage name since leaving Neon Nights. This suspicion of mine was also supported by the detectives' physical description. Of course, that didn't get us very far, because I still had to get her to talk somehow.
"She will talk," Matt said. "She just needs a big shot she's willing to talk to."
"Is that what she said?" I asked back. "What did she say exactly?"
"That she won't talk to detectives, especially not if Neon Nights is the subject. She wanted someone she trusts to contact her."
"And who could it be? Jess...?" I inquired, then pretended to suddenly think of something else before adding, "...ica." The two detectives were not fazed.
"She wants to speak with the prosecutor."
"Interesting..." I cut it short. "Why is it better for her if she talks to me?"

Jake Cooper lived in the worst neighborhood of the city. The roads leading there were often bordered by actual mountains of garbage. One had the feeling as if the waste collected in the other half of the city was dumped here. It was more likely, however, that even the garbage collectors steered well clear of this neighborhood. I was surprised that Jake Cooper's address was in this place.
"Where did you find this address?" I asked the detectives somewhat accusingly.
"A source of ours tipped us off," they answered.
"And is that source trying to screw with you on purpose?"
"Don't worry, the address is correct," Matt answered.

"We understand you're worried," Wilbur continued. "You don't need to be afraid with us around. There are neighborhoods like this, people live here too. They are more afraid of you than you are of them."

Jake Cooper's house was a single-story prefabricated house. At some point there might have been a small garden in front of it; now rusty barrels stood askew, surrounded by all kinds of metal junk. In front of the house stood a sun-bleached yellowish lounge chair; the umbrella must have been blown away by time long ago, if there ever was one. From the outside, it didn't look like anyone lived here.

Wilbur got out of the car and looked around the house. Matt stayed with me in the meantime. I really was afraid. I wasn't used to such neighborhoods; besides, a few people had ventured out onto the street. When they saw the detectives' car, they stared for minutes. We caused no small stir; they knew exactly who didn't belong here. Wilbur went up to a few of them.
"Someone lives there," he said as he got back into the car.
"It doesn't look like it," I replied.
"They haven't seen him for weeks."
"And is that Jake Cooper?" I inquired.
"They didn't tell me his name, but I could tell they knew him."
"And do you believe them?"
"They don't lie about things like that. Even if they say otherwise, the truth is plain to see. They're always protecting someone."

Unfortunate people. Are they truly more afraid of us than the other way around? The detectives were certainly right. A scary exterior can stem from many things: illnesses, addictions. It is the person living in misery who ends up despised by everyone. What can someone do who is born here? This will be home for them, and they won't understand the other world around them. Everything will be foreign to them; only this misery, this will be familiar. What can get someone out of here? What kind of dreams do you have to believe in to escape? Jake Cooper had a dream. And to free himself, he had to ensnare us.
"We must find this man," I said, though I hated the very thought of speaking to him.
"We'll watch the place," Wilbur promised. "If he shows up, we'll bring him in."
"I'm afraid he'll run if we aren't careful enough."
"Or he already has," Matt suggested.
"No!" I replied. "How could he have known we'd look for him? He will return if he lives here."
Suddenly, a text message interrupted the conversation.
"Miss Evans!" Matt said. "Our guy just sent over the Alioglu family's address."
"Already?" I was surprised.
"It's pretty close to here, want to check it out?"
"Absolutely!" I replied, my heart suddenly pounding in my throat.

I felt this lead was hotter than the others. I didn't know how thoroughly they had investigated Mike's case, but if Neon Nights had indeed been mentioned in connection with it, I wouldn't have been surprised if they had wrapped up the investigation prematurely. I hoped the family might still share some information that the police hadn't taken seriously enough, which could bring us closer to who Mike was in contact with in the organization.

The Alioglu family's house was ten minutes from Jake Cooper's suspected home, albeit in the same district. This already counted as a better neighborhood; the feeling of fear also subsided in me, and I had to realize that my weapon only promised false security, since I didn't want to use it at all. Here, however, it didn't even cross my mind that it was on me; I got out of the car immediately as we stopped. The street was lined with plane trees, giving it a suburban atmosphere.

In front of the house, a clothesline was stretched across, but in the damp, wet weather, only water droplets dried on it. The light was already on in the window; it was slowly getting dark. I knocked, while the two detectives served as backup behind me. A heavyset woman of about fifty opened the door.
"Good day!" I greeted her. "Is this the Alioglu house?"
The woman stared at us with narrowed eyes, nodding uncertainly.
"I'm Amanda Evans, the prosecutor. These gentlemen behind me are detectives. We'd like to ask you a few questions."
"About what?" the woman asked, confused.
"About the death of Mike Alioglu."
Her large frame shuddered slightly; with fear in her eyes, she made no move to open the door any wider.
"Mike died a long time ago. Why should we still talk about him?"
"His name came up in another investigation," I replied.
"I don't think so. He was a good boy. He wouldn't hurt a fly. You're looking for the wrong person."
I understood the mother's reaction, and was filled with the same compassion I had felt when reading Mike's file.
"Then tell me who we should look for instead."
The woman stared the floor, then decided to let us in after all.
"Come in! Just don't touch anything!"

Her warning might have seemed like an exaggeration, but looking around the room, I understood better why she said it. A huge number of items were tastefully arranged on the shelves. It must have taken hours to tidy up, which she might do daily. Three young people sat on the living room sofa, and who knows how many more lived here. She said something to them in a loud voice in Turkish, and they retreated to another room.

"Have a seat," she offered, and the three of us sat down side by side on the sofa. "Coffee!" she barked to whoever could hear her, and two of them immediately jumped up to bring us some. None of us objected. A warm, family atmosphere filled the room; it felt almost nice.
"Thank you," I said on behalf of all of us. "Please forgive us for barging in on you like this, but we really need to know more about Mike's death."
"Why?" she asked back.
"Reflecting on the crowd he got mixed up with, we need to understand the situation."
"I see," she acknowledged. "Then I will tell the police for the last time that Mike was not the kind of person they tried to portray him as."
"What kind of person was he, and what kind of person did they try to portray him as?" I inquired.
"You didn't handle his case, did you?" she looked at Wilbur.
"No. We got onto this from a completely different direction."

The kids set the coffee down in front of us and left. Their mother took a deep breath; it was obvious how much she dreaded talking about Mike's death again, perhaps also fearing she would only reopen old wounds for nothing, without achieving anything anyway.

"Mike was a good boy. He was a huge help to me. Of course, no matter how much I told everyone that, they just kept repeating that he got mixed up with the wrong crowd, and that's why he died. But it wasn't true."
"Why are you so sure of that?" I asked, somewhat provocatively—a question I had absolutely no right to ask in the eyes of a mother.
"Because I knew him," she replied concisely and firmly.
"Teenagers have secrets from their parents."
My comment didn't make the woman lose her patience. She called out to one of her sons. When he came closer, she questioned him.
"Where were you yesterday at six in the evening?"
The boy replied with a grin on his face.
"With Zake and Melissa in the parking lot."
"And what did you do?"
"We smoked, talked. We ate hot dogs. The vendor raised the price."
"How much?" the mother asked.
"50 cents."
"Who else was there?"
"A lot of people. The Brighton Twins."
"Is Sue still obsessed with you?"
"If that changes, I'll let you know," he smiled.
"You can go."
He wasn't embarrassed by his mother's questions; it seemed their relationship was completely normal.
"That was Daniel. He's a bit of a trickster, but he's honest. I might not always know where he is, but if I ask, he'll tell me. I have a good relationship with my kids."
"I see," I cut in.

"Mike was not like that. You didn't have to pry things out of him. He was like an angel. Even as a little boy, if someone hurt a bug, the poor kid would be completely distraught. There was no more sensitive soul on this earth than him."
"I believe you," I replied. "But for some reason he died. What do you think could have happened?"
"I don't know for sure, but I know who would."
"And who?"
"The witness whom the police questioned. He was there, so I'm sure he knows what happened, he just told it differently."
"Why did he do that?" I asked.
"Because he was afraid. First they said he might have killed him, obviously he was scared shitless. He started talking about all sorts of things."
"Do you think he lied?" I inquired.
"He just hid the truth: that he was the one who wanted to join that organization."
"Which organization?" I asked. I wanted to hear her say the obvious.
"Neon Nights. You know, that hooker joint."
It felt good to hear those words from someone else's lips. I felt there was at least one person who knew what a terrible place Neon Nights was without ever having stepped foot inside.
"But ask around the neighborhood. Everyone knows that organization was fishing around here."
"What do you mean?"
"Isn't it clear?" she countered. "There were plenty of young boys around here who wanted money. They were constantly trying to recruit them to work for them."
"Do you know what kind of work they were recruiting them for?"
"No. I don't know that. But it was definitely something shady. A lot of them fell for it. Mike was worried about them."
"Mike was worried about them?"
"I told you before how sensitive he was. Of course he worried. He grew up with a lot of them. I think that night he wanted to play the hero."

Based on the mother's account, a completely different picture of the boy emerged before me, and I couldn't see why Mike Alioglu couldn't have been exactly as she described. Why couldn't he have been a decent, sensitive guy who, unlike the others, understood that there could be no such thing as easy, high-paying work, especially not in this neighborhood? I believed his mother when she said Mike had been worried about his friends.
"What was Mike like? Physically," I inquired.
"Gorgeous," the mother replied. "He was strong, with a handsome face. I'm sure all the girls liked him."
"Did the others look up to him?"
"He was a popular boy. Yes, I think they listened to him."
"What do you think happened that night? What did you mean by saying he wanted to play the hero?"
I wanted to reconstruct the scene, and I figured the mother had a far more accurate picture of that night in her mind than what the police had written down in the interrogation reports.

"There was this friend of his. He worried about him a lot. He told me the boy had got in touch with those people. He didn't say what they lured him with, only that they offered him a very high-paying job. He knew Mike wanted to find work too, to help out at home. I didn't insist on it; we got by. The other boy, however, kept pushing, insisting it would be great. Mike saw right through them and wanted to talk him out of it at all costs, but couldn't. So he thought he'd approach the matter from another angle."
"Is that why Mike met with the Neon Nights people?"

"Apparently, yes." The mother stared at the floor for a few seconds. She fell silent. I could almost see her conjuring up the image of her son. "He shouldn't have been there. I have no idea what he was thinking. He must have spoken to them; I think he wanted to get through to them, to make them leave this neighborhood. I don't think it ever crossed his mind that he could get hurt. The whole thing made no sense. Mike couldn't have been a threat to them. He was just a local boy who liked living here and loved his friends. Those people couldn't understand that, because they were barbarians."

I didn't even know what to say. I felt the mother's pain. Her son's death was senseless, and the way they killed him was pure cruelty. I could only hope that in time, it would come to light who did it.
"Are you sure it happened that way?" I asked, since she had put it so convincingly.
"No," she replied instantly. "I'm not sure. But the story is a thousand times more believable this way than the version the police came up with."
"Then where did you get all this from?"
"Mike's friend told us at the funeral."
"Then why did he tell the police a different story?"
"Because he was afraid, Miss Evans. He was barely sixteen. He was terrified of something happening to him."
"Yet he did tell them about Neon Nights."
"Yes, he did. He had every reason to."
"Wasn't he afraid they'd retaliate?"

"No, he didn't worry about that. He knew perfectly well that if Neon Nights was mentioned, the police would close the case as quickly as possible, and since they had no evidence against him, they'd leave him alone."
"A clever move," Matt noted unexpectedly. The mother just stared blankly ahead.
"And you just let the matter rest?" I asked, puzzled.

"I didn't blame him. Mike would have wanted him to stay safe, too. People stick together around here. He didn't want to hurt Mike. And what good would it have done if I pushed? I only knew what Jake had told me anyway."
"Who?" I asked, my voice dropping. In the blink of an eye, all my energy drained away. Mrs. Alioglu immediately noticed my reaction.
"Are you all right, prosecutor?"
"Mike's friend was Jake Cooper?" I asked nervously.
"Yes, Miss Evans," she replied calmly. "From the looks of it, he's the one you're searching for."

My mind was spinning, my emotions in turmoil. Jake Cooper was the witness from whose perspective I had learned about the events, and as it turned out, he had presented a completely distorted version of the truth to me. Now, more than ever, I wanted to meet him, look him in the eye, and see if he recognized me. After he recruited us, we never spoke again, not even once. He hadn't become a gentleman. I didn't know where he had vanished to, or what had become of him. I basically knew nothing about him, yet he had changed the entire course of my life.

At first, I hadn't thought of him as an important player, yet everywhere I turned, I stumbled into him. He was like a phantom. I had no idea what he actually did, or what his role had been in how things played out; he was simply there.

At the same time, a sense of calm washed over me. I felt a circle had closed—one that could have gone on forever, but instead had taken mercy, choosing not to drag me deeper into the labyrinth. I had to speak with him. I had to find out what role he had played in everything that happened to us.

If Mike had lived, maybe everything would have turned out differently. Maybe Jess and I would never have ended up at Neon Nights, and a different, easier life would have been waiting for us. But I didn't want to fool myself. In our desperation, someone else would have eventually found us and, like Jake, got us in there, since at the time we saw no other escape from our home.
"Mike would have just turned thirty," Mrs. Alioglu said after a short pause. "How old are you?" she asked point-blank.
From her tone, I sensed she was asking more than just that.
"Twenty-five," I replied.
"Very young," she noted. "Two years younger than the boys."

"I don't feel young," I countered. "I've already been through a lot in my life. The fact that I'm not yet thirty doesn't mean anything. I stopped seeing the world through rose-colored glasses a long time ago."
"Oh, of course you don't," she replied. "You seem like a determined woman. You know exactly what you want, and also why."
"Why are you telling me this?" I was puzzled.
She didn't answer.
"When was the last time you saw Jake?" I asked.
"At the funeral or not long after."
"That long ago?"
"Yes, that was the last time."
"But do you know if Jake still lives around here?"
"Sure, though to tell you the truth, I haven't heard anything about him in a long time. I'd rather say I only know that he used to live here."
"Do you know where?"
"Somewhere by the numbered streets."
"Have you been there?"
"In the neighborhood, yes. But not at their house. I didn't know his parents. He only came over because of Mike."
"How is it that you still remember him so well?"
"I don't think you're asking that seriously," she answered, and she was right. I actually just wanted to make sure she was telling the truth. Mrs. Alioglu stood up and walked over to a cabinet.
"Could I ask a favor of you?" she asked.
"What is it?"
She pulled out a photo of Mike.
"If you find Jake, would you give him this picture?"
"Why?" I asked, finding the request strange.
"Just give it to him, please."

There was something touching in her voice. I had no idea what was going through her mind, but I didn't want to pry. I looked at the picture. A very handsome, dark-eyed, cheerful boy smiled back at me. He was barely sixteen.

chapters.title: Chapter Ten
paragraphs: January 26, 2022
In the morning, a message was waiting on my phone. Jessica sent it. It was just a picture and a sentence: "Fuck them!". I zoomed in on the picture and immediately handed it to Anton.
"Look!"
"Is this another threat?" he asked, as if he had sensed it.
"That's what it looks like."
"Then withdraw the complaint!" he said immediately.
"Ugh," I protested. "Fuck them!"
I called Jess immediately.
"Where did you find it?" I asked.
"In the mailbox, this one too."
"Aren't they tired of it yet?"
In the background, I heard a man's voice arguing, then he took the phone from Jessica.
"Miss Evans?!"
"Yes."
Jefferson had been dating Jess for years, but naturally, I had never seen him. I had no idea who he was. Now he was distraught, speaking almost in a shout.
"I don't know how long you intend to play with fire, but stop it! Let this whole thing end! We are moving somewhere far away. We are not going to live like this!"
"I understand," I replied calmly, surprising even myself by how much. "Please hand the phone back to Jessica."
"Jessica," I said, "we have the option of having you withdraw the complaint."
"But then I can't file it again," she replied.
"That's true, but we can. You can still testify just the same."
"I will only discredit the whole thing with that, Miss Evans."
"Withdraw it under the influence of threats. This might even strengthen our position."
"I'm not afraid of them!" she insisted. "I'm not going to back down. It's like former colleagues want to silence me."
Jessica paused.
"I'll think about it," she answered finally. "My fiancé is truly unbearable when he worries. I swear, that's going to be the main reason I do it."
"Do it, Jessica, leave the rest to us!" I reassured her. "Also, since we're speaking, could you perhaps talk to David King?"
"Why me?" she asked back.
"I feel he is uncertain. I fear he won't want to testify."
"It's ironic that you ask me this precisely when you want me to withdraw the complaint."
"But I don't want to drop the case, Jessica!" I defended myself.
"It doesn't matter anyway..."
Anton suddenly reached for my phone and hung up.
"What are you doing?!" I yelled at him.
"There's no point in you two fighting now."
"We fight when we want to," I replied, but I didn't call Jessica back; I just walked away from Anton and went into the bathroom.
Jessica was being completely unreasonable. I hated when someone tried to paint me as selfish. I knew Jess didn't think that, yet the sarcasm with which she emphasized her last sentence bit into me.

Jeff might have overreacted to the situation, though his fear could be understood. He only knew Neon Nights from stories, so he could expect anything from them. To tell the truth, I didn't really believe Jessica's life was in danger either, but it was possible that we underestimated their baseness.

The fact that they had been threatened, however, made no sense to me. Every day I received the reports, and after a quick query, it turned out that the police assigned to watch the house didn't notice any movement around Jessica's house during the night. Thinking it over, however, several methods presented themselves for someone to deliver the threatening message to Jessica's mailbox, and it wasn't important to catch a courier, but that Jess wouldn't be harmed.
Even if I was only making things harder for Neon Nights by keeping them there, it was worth it. Jess could take care of herself anyway.

Regardless, I really hoped that she would finally agree and do what was necessary. I felt everything would become easier from it, especially since we were just beginning to dig deeper into the leads unfolding before us.
Anton timidly tried to approach me, but I rejected him.
"Do you think this is the right moment for this?" I asked condescendingly.

He slinked away as if nothing else mattered in life besides sex. I didn't understand how it even occurred to him after this morning. Before the message, of course, he would still have had the opportunity, but so much had happened since! Any mood for it had dissolved in the morning fog.
"I'm going to Hermione's," I said.
"Okay, good luck!" he replied with excessive kindness. I felt he wasn't sincere, but he restrained himself.

I realized that was my problem with his approach too. He was wishy-washy, like an idiot. If he had really wanted me, he would have just taken me. And yet, right now it would have felt so good to feel wanted. Jessica's guy was whining, and mine had had the chance to step up and prove himself, but he blew it. If he had just made me his, at least I would have felt safe... but men can be so stupid sometimes.

Hermione lived in the kind of place where I could see myself living. I wouldn't have traded our suburban house for an apartment, but I could have gotten used to the doorman at our gate. Even if he was annoyingly self-important, forcing me to shut him up by showing my badge. After this morning, say, I wasn't sure I didn't have a greater need for this.
I wasn't wrong about Hermione. I did know her. Standing in the doorway opposite me was Mary Morales.
"Come in!" she said in a very warm and familiar tone.
"I'm prosecutor Amanda Evans," I greeted her, ignoring the obvious fact that she already knew who I was.
"Amanda Evans..." she laughed. "You're Alice. Alice Bucks. You don't think I forgot your voice, do you?" She practically jumped at me to hug me.

It was hard for me to react to what happened. For a moment I grew even angrier at Jessica, because I thought she might have told her that I was the one who would look for her. During the conversation, however, it turned out that Jess hadn't spoken to Mary for years.
"How did you know it was me?" I asked finally, because I saw no point in denying it.

"The two detectives you sent here tried to persuade me to talk. They brought up the prosecutor leading the investigation, and from a few of their words it became clear that it could only be you. You always said you'd have them locked up one day. Of course, many people make irresponsible promises, but when I went blind, I remember you were the first to come to me. Blood was pouring from my head. I wasn't completely conscious, but it burned into me how you said it. I knew you meant it seriously."

I was almost embarrassed by this warm welcome, of course it was good that Mary remembered this moment and took it seriously. I really got there first. Poor Mary fell against the glass table, which completely shattered. Her back and arm were shredded by the glass shards. Although our sessions were often so intense that a horse race would have envied the pace, it was still unusual for the furniture to end up destroyed. We knew it wasn't an accident. Mary's face was covered in blood. The fat bastard was sweating and panting over her with a broken champagne bottle in his hand. He wasn't wearing pants, his cock was still hard, and all I could think about was putting that sharp glass into him instead of Neon Nights' most exquisite beauty. The client was led out by the gentleman, and then somehow they settled the matter between themselves. Of course, Mary had seen nothing of it. Nor from the hush money they paid for it as compensation.
"Look Mary, no one can find out who I am."
"Don't worry about that," she answered. "I certainly won't tell anyone. I didn't talk to the detectives either."
"Do you know why I came?"
"Actually, no. But if you introduced yourself as prosecutor Amanda Evans, you can only want to fulfill your promise."
"Yes, that's true," I replied.
"But why do you need me for this?" she asked.
"You know why I need you. To testify."
"Of course, gladly," she said immediately, as if there were no tomorrow.
I was slightly surprised. Mary hadn't even hesitated.
"You're saying yes already?" I said in disbelief.
"Yes. Why wouldn't I?"
"Don't you want to think it through?"
"What should I think through? You want to punish those who abused and exploited us for so many years. Do you know how long I've been waiting for this?"
I didn't know.
"Since when?"
"What kind of question is that? Since you first said it. I believed you. And lo and behold, now you stand here, calling me to testify."

I felt strange, as if this whole thing embarrassed me. When I came here, we were still at the point where I had to convince someone named Hermione to speak at all. And now, a moment later, I already had a witness.
"You need to know what you're getting yourself into," I began, because I felt Mary didn't see the situation completely realistically, but she interrupted.
"Alice! Or rather Amanda... I better practice this name of yours."
"Yes, let it be Amanda just to keep things clean," I replied, then heard how condescending it sounded. I wanted to clarify: "Alice is dead."
"You died?" Mary wondered.
"Yes," I replied shortly, but my voice was far from firm, rather some deep sadness. I felt sorry for Alice. "Alice died, more precisely."
"Amanda. I know what you are asking. You don't have to worry about me."
"Jessica was threatened twice," I emphasized the validity of my fear.
"We all know what they are like," she snapped. "And I hate them!" Sparks flew from her blind eyes. "I hate them, do you understand?!"
"I understand," I replied shortly, because how could I not.
I understood, though I could never know what she had gone through. Even though she went blind, she worked just the same. No one cared what happened.

"I know what you believe now," she explained. "But I felt only hatred for them even before they did this to me. This really didn't change anything. That I went blind? What does it matter. What did it matter there whether you see or not? Sometimes you might even have envied me for it. All those disgusting pieces of shit we were with. They wanted slaves so they could do everything."
"They knew we were."

"And that turned them on. That prick, do you remember him? You were there too. We weren't exactly new to the business back then. Was I supposed to apologize for not gagging on him? That it wasn't big enough to strangle me? He took offense at being laughed at. 'Live happily with it, man,' I said, 'but you don't need to think you're Rocco.' He couldn't have been used to someone speaking to him as if he were mortal too, so he hit me on the head. I wasn't scared. I had no plans back then."
"I remember," I replied, "and you're saying even now you have nothing to risk?"
"There is nothing I'm afraid of losing."
"What do you do, Mary?" I inquired. "Who is Hermione?"
"The witch from Harry Potter."
"Do you perform magic?"
"According to many, yes. Though I don't even meet them."
A sudden realization dawned on me.
"Mary, am I right in thinking you're on the webcam..."
"Spot on!" she cut into my words, as she had done several times already, then grabbed my arm and led me toward her bedroom.

In the middle of the room was a huge white bed covered with a pink blanket, decorated with puffy throw pillows. On the wall, pink textile leather inserts enhanced the atmosphere, which was made truly complete by the white canopy surrounding the bed. Opposite the bed, the unsuspecting visitor could inspect a professional camera system, and if that hadn't blinded them completely, the two studio spotlights certainly achieved it.
"Holy shit, Mary, you work here?!" I was surprised, a laugh tinged with awe mixing into my voice.
"Do you like it?" she asked back with a proud smile on her lips.
"Well, I don't even know what to say," I replied.
"Amanda, you haven't become a prude, have you?" she complained teasingly. "What is a person supposed to live on? I'm a star," she admitted.
"I'm sure of that," I replied honestly. If there was one thing the girl understood, it was sex.
"And do guys come here?" I inquired.
"What a boomer you are! That's all I need! They're on the other side of the screen. I don't need them here. I'm just having fun. I enjoy it. I love it all."

For minutes I just walked around the room with a confused smile. It was lucky she couldn't see it, otherwise she really might have thought I was a prude. Mary was still beautiful and I could believe she was casting a spell. There were at least thirty different naughty variations of costumes hanging in the closets, from Harley Quinn to Snow White. The schoolgirl set had an almost ordinary effect.
"Mary, it's good to see you," I commended. "You look good, and you know what to do with yourself."

"One does what they are best at. Morals, I think, we stripped off quite a long time ago, and if one can live this well off it, it certainly doesn't bother me. Besides, I do it the way it's good for me."
"And really, no one comes here?"
"A few good friends," she replied. "But they are truly good friends. And they only give what's needed."

Mary's eyes sparkled with life, despite clearly staring into nothingness. The blow hit her temple. It wasn't her eyes that were damaged, but the optic nerve. They looked as if they were made of dark chocolate.
"And are you well?" she asked somewhat unexpectedly, though if I had thought about it at that moment, I could have known it was my turn.
"Yes," I replied shortly. "You see, I'm working on the case of my life."
"That's truly impressive."
"How do you mean?"
"I have no doubt that this is your biggest case. But that is exactly why I'm sure it didn't start today. Not even a few weeks ago, nor even a few months ago."
"To tell the truth, on the 13th."
"No. That's not how I meant it."
"Yes, I know," I replied. "But I couldn't have done it alone. I owe a lot to Anton."
"Who is he?" she was curious.
"Anton is the opposite of Neon Nights in everything. It's ironic that I still met him there."
"You got together with a client?" she was surprised.
"Client? No way. At least not in that sense. I don't even know how he ended up there anymore. I didn't even sleep with him. He was simply there and fell in love with me."

It happened so long ago, and before so much else, that it became completely irrelevant how we met. Anton just stared at me as if he hadn't seen a naked woman before, he was like a little boy, though he was much older than me. It was his first time in a nightclub. "You started in the best place!" I told him. "Still, how on earth did you wander in here, you innocent kid?" That's what I felt. I almost got embarrassed that I had no clothes on. Everyone saw only a naked body that turned them on, and he saw a girl who was afraid.
"Anton is a writer," I continued. "Anton Martin. In the last few years, he has had quite a lot of success. He writes crime stories. He has believed in me since he met me."
"I guess a dream of his came true, dating a prosecutor."
"He never expressed it that way, but I hope so."

I didn't know what to say more. Mary's presence reassured me unusually, and this filled me with a truly good feeling. Meeting an old acquaintance, strangely, didn't evoke the worst moments of our years together, but rather a close bond I had to trust.
