cold blue

chapters.title: Chapter Nineteen
paragraphs: March 8, 2022

The president did not resign. Only, as he phrased it, he suspended his office for the duration of the investigation. His place was taken by one of his vice presidents—which one is essentially all the same. This of course was not said by him; I thought of it. His stepping into the background was necessary so that the authorities could investigate the slanders brought against him undisturbed. It was strange to hear this in this form, since the same authority "slandered" him as was dealing with the investigation of the case. Regardless, it sounded good.

The next day at the prosecution briefing, I found myself facing a real team. In the task force there were detectives, prosecutors, experts, communication specialists on whom the task fell to make our work go as undisturbed as possible. A more important topic than the trial against the president could hardly be provided by anyone at the present moment, so we prepared for an intrusive media presence. Wright forbade us from giving statements to anyone in the case; besides her, only communication staff could leak information to the public. In one day, interest took on huge proportions. Everyone spoke of it, the opposition organized demonstrations, a host of political experts gave interviews on various platforms, producing multi-million views instead of previous hundreds of thousands.

It was hard to stay calm. I was constantly scrolling my mobile and trying to assess the consequences of this negotiation, while I felt the pressure increasing. The politics of previous years may be in jeopardy, declared a political scientist, whose justification for the statement I could no longer read, because the title of another article in the news feed also caught my attention. The term presidential pardon takes on a new meaning. And indeed, as clickbait as it seemed, there was truth in it. Although the president had the power to pardon anyone, I knew he didn't deserve the same. The two interpretations began to blur together in my head, but with great difficulty I managed to turn off my phone screen before I was completely screwed. I took a deep breath. I need a dumb phone, I thought. And I put the mobile as deep as possible in my pocket.

The next moment, I already found myself walking in the hallway of the prosecutor's office. I tried to get out to the yard to freshen up, but a colleague, with an unknown man at his side, addressed me.
"Amanda, this gentleman is Jessica Marsh's lawyer," he said.
"Bill Thompson," the person introduced himself.
I was very surprised. Jessica never said she had her own lawyer.
"Evans," I answered. "What can I help you with?"
"It's a bit of a weird situation," he started. "I want to hand over a message for you from Jessica Marsh."
My eyes opened wide.
"A letter to be exact."
"That indeed is strange," I said, "because Jessica Marsh is dead."
"Of course," he replied with the greatest respect. "I know that too; regardless, the letter comes from her. Can we talk?"
The man was middle-aged. Slightly stocky, wearing a checkered suit. If I had to describe a civil lawyer, I would have thought of similar.
"I was just heading out to the yard for a walk, you can join me," I said.
"We can do the signing out there as well," he replied.
"Do I have to sign it?"
"Just a formality, obviously."
The lawyer spoke slowly and politely. While we got out, I learned that he wanted to get home for lunch. It was noon. I didn't think we had to talk for too long; after all, it was only about a letter.
"Jessica approached me with a strange request a few months ago," he started.
"Since when do you know her?" I asked.
"Quite a long time. It's been five years now," he replied. "We could say I'm her lawyer, as I also took the liberty of telling your colleague."
"Can we just say?"
"Well," he sighed, "you know, she paid my monthly retainer constantly, but she didn't ask for any legal help from me at all."
"That's interesting," I noted.

"Now and then she came to my place for tea, but even then it didn't seem like she needed my work. Of course, she was interested in things, such as how much legal support for the purchase of an apartment would cost, but I never once had to represent her in any matter."
"Did you just go for tea then?" I was confused. I knew Jessica well, but nothing would have been further from her than such tea stirrings. The lawyer obviously couldn't know that.

"I thought it would surprise you," he answered. "I'm sorry to talk to you like this, but from what Jessica asked, I was sure that you two knew each other, so I said that because I thought it would surprise you."
The thing was beginning to get confusing.

"Unfortunately, you are mistaken," I denied the situation, because although the lawyer seemed very friendly, this was still one of our biggest secrets with Jessica, especially now that things had turned critical.
"Well, it happens to me too," he replied.
"Still, it's strange that she paid your monthly retainer, yet only went over to have tea."
"We talked a lot."
"I'm sorry," I interrupted, "but can we get to the actual reason you came here?"

"Yes, my apologies," he said apologetically, as if it were the most natural thing in the world. "On one occasion—it must have been October—she stopped by for more than just a cup of tea. She said that if she were to die for any reason..."
"If she died?" I cut in. "In October she was already talking about what should happen if she died?"

"Yes. That's why I said she turned to me with a strange request," he said. "Of course, it's completely normal if someone wants a will drawn up, but Jessica was not even thirty, and she didn't come because of that."
"Do you think she might have thought she was going to be killed?" I asked because that was the first thing that came to mind.
"Or that she was suffering from some illness. Seeing the facts, however, I see more chance of the first."
"But Jessica had an accident," I explained, since this was the official position. "Didn't you ask her why she was preparing for this eventuality?"

"I reacted similarly to you. Then, with a pitying smile on her face, she made it clear to me that what she was doing was very timely. So she handed me two letters and asked me to hand them over to you if it happened."
"Me specifically?"

"Yes, that's why I brought it here; I must give it to the prosecutor of the case against the president," he replied. "Despite the fact," now he made a small dramatic pause, "that she didn't even know you."
"This indeed is interesting. And why did you only bring one letter?"
"Because I can only hand over the other after—and here I quote Jessica literally," he excused himself again, "'when Amanda finally puts that prick in prison.'"
I almost laughed. Bill Thompson also felt how ill-suited this word was to him, which was why he tried to distance himself as much as possible from the quote's style.
"And do you know what is in the letters?" I asked.
"No, by no means! I respected Jessica's request, and these messages are not addressed to me, but to you."
"Thank you so much for bringing it," I said, signing my name on the dotted line. I couldn't wait to open it. I had no idea what was in it.

"You are very welcome," he replied. "I won't trouble you any longer," he said, taking his leave. "I hope we meet again," he continued his somewhat fragmented speech, "but in any case, yes, good luck!" We shook hands and he left.
We shook hands and he left.
A few moments later, however, he appeared in the doorway again.
"Miss Evans!"
"Yes?"
"Jessica asked me to tell you: cuckoo."
I stared blankly. I didn't understand anything.
"What did she ask?" I asked back.
"To tell you: cuckoo," Bill spread his arms. "I don't understand it either. I hoped you would."
"Well, no," I replied, puzzled.
"If you ever need help, call me!" the lawyer offered his services.
"Thank you," I smiled at him, but didn't understand how he could be of help to me.
I sat down on one of the benches and opened Jessica's message.
Fuck these faggots!
Hi Amy!

"I don't think I could have started the letter otherwise. Believe me, it's not out of my own good will that I'm not here. It would have been better to speak in person, but that's how it is. That's life. However we want to control it, at most we can ride on it.

This letter is a sort of insurance because I don't know when what I expect will happen. I need a letter in which I write down everything about the years spent in the Neon Nights. You know everything, of course, since you were there, and I told you everything about the period when you weren't, too. Take this as a written deposition for the trial. I wanted to report these in person, but apparently things worked out differently..."

Here Jess described at length and in detail on separate sheets everything that happened in the Neon Nights, including how she blackmailed the president into closing the club. To foreign ears it will certainly sound fascinating, I thought. I blessed my luck that the information was not lost after all. All the bad feeling that arose because of Jess's ease—that she didn't speak of the information regarding the closing of Neon Nights before the detectives—vanished in one swoop.
At the end of the letter stood a few more lines.

You can trust Bill. You know we know each other. I told him, but he would never abuse that. He is a very good person. He really is, not just pretending. I'm only saying this so that if you ever need to use it for something, don't be afraid to turn to him.

You should say goodbye. My arm is dying from writing so much. Anyway, I could only write nonsense, to say; I've been missing you for years and I'm afraid we'll never be the same again. And that; too bad I can't be there when you put that bastard in jail!
Don't worry about any of it! The first one really doesn't matter and the second one is your destiny.
i love you
Jess"

I struggled with my tears, but I didn't care; no one saw me anyway. I was glad of the letter; it saved my ass. The strange circumstances, however, I couldn't place. Why did Jessica already know her life was in danger when no one could have known about the complaint yet? Why didn't she speak? Why did she need this lawyer? Why did she go to have tea with him? And what didn't fit in my head in the least: what does it mean: cuckoo?

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty
paragraphs: March 9, 2022

The team worked hard. I contacted both Hermione and David King to tell them Jessica was dead. Both were touched by the news, but King still didn't know if he would be willing to testify. Despite my persuasion, he didn't want to give in; he just kept saying that he had to think about it some more. However, this was less important than before.

When news of the proceedings against the president spread, several people voluntarily approached the police to tell their own stories. Previously, Jess and I were afraid of who the media coverage would favor, since the president had very influential acquaintances. However, I hoped that the truth could make better use of the power of the public than manipulation, and this was also indicated by the recent confessions.

However, Mortenstein's was still missing. Even though it has been a week since what he did became public, he still hasn't spoken out, and he couldn't just be taken to the police, because that would have damaged his political reputation. Several media still treated the situation as if the report was based on speculation. The presidential office was obviously trying to communicate this to the public, and the fact that it took a step back even made it sympathetic to many. However, I was not so forgiving. The hatred in me was growing every day, and the interviews with his supporters didn't help. One by one, the accusations made were classified as slander, and I had the impression that all our statements would be subjected to tremendous pressure, which would aim to unsettle the public. Regardless, I trusted the prosecutor's office, knowing that Wright would do everything to make this case run as smoothly as possible, even if the attorney general was known to be one of the president's proteges.

I was reading the new statements in the privacy of my desk when Matt called and asked me to go to his police station because one of the witnesses had a particularly interesting story to tell. It sounded exciting.
While on guard, I tried to think about how they could catch us. I was alert. I knew the president's strategy was to attack, even if he was now feigning retreat.

The girl sitting in the interrogation room was not familiar at all. Of course, that meant nothing. I didn't recognize David King either. Her blonde hair was down to her waist, her nails were studded with stones, and the clothes she wore were worth five thousand. Either she started a very good career after Neon Nights, or she was very happily married, I thought. In any case, there was something classy in her movements, and I got the feeling that she didn't learn all this with us; she could always have been like that.

"I consider him my supporter to this day," she answered the investigator's question about her relationship with the president. "I can thank Mr. Mortenstein for preparing me for my career abroad. Without the courses at Neon Nights, I certainly wouldn't have made it to New York and worked with the best designers week after week."
"What is your occupation?" asked the detective.
"I am a model."
"Let's clarify then. What is your relationship with President Edgar Mortenstein?"

"Look, I don't know how much I can talk about this, since I signed a non-disclosure agreement that year, which gave the trainings exclusivity, but I think that in this delicate situation, maybe I can still say this or that."
"An indictment is being prepared against the president, so I think if you know anything about the things the complaint is about, don't keep it to yourself!"
"That will be for the best," the girl acknowledged.

I looked at Matt, shaking my leg nervously. Just what kind of training programs is she talking about? He must have thought the same, because incomprehension sat on his face. We had listened through quite a few testimonies together, but none of them spoke of anything similar.
"I'm glad you called me," I thanked him while we watched the witness through the interrogator's spyglass.
The girl continued.

"My father has known Mortenstein for a long time. Even as a child I met him many times at various receptions. He was always very kind; I have a good relationship with one of his sons, we've been friends since then, so to speak, even if life drifted us far apart. He always knew I was interested in fashion, how much the glittering world attracted me. I was fourteen, just starting high school, when Edgar offered my father that I could participate in one of Neon Nights' exclusive training programs, which started specifically for girls like me."
"What do you mean by girls like you?" the detective asked.
"Attractive girls who are, of course, interested in fashion," she summarized how she defined her fourteen-year-old self.
"Did you have anything else in common?"
"What do you mean?"
"Say, that you knew the president."

"No, no. Definitely not," the girl protested. "Many of us didn't meet him at all. I was obviously in a privileged position in this respect, but the president had no say in the training programs whatsoever. He was only the visionary of Neon Nights' glamour."
"Glamour?"
"They always said: shine, and believe in yourselves, because then others will see it too. This was the first thing they drilled into us there."
"So the Neon Nights was a modeling school?"

"Like I said, I signed a nondisclosure agreement, but maybe they'll understand if I talk about it openly," she tossed her blonde hair back, then gathered her thoughts and continued. "I wouldn't call it a model trainer. Rather, a place where they are aware of how to turn a girl into a successful woman, and the focus is on the woman. Everything revolved around that. We had mentors who had already achieved a lot in their profession and were ready to pass on the knowledge they had accumulated to the younger generation. I was taught by real celebrities like Leona St. Claire, and I hardly need a better model than her."
"What else did you learn?" the detective inquired.
"A great many things. Etiquette, dance, acting, conversation. But there were those who learned music, singing, or other knowledge that a cultured and educated woman might need."
"And what was the goal of these training programs?"

"Are you paying attention to me at all?" the girl complained. "I told you earlier. The goal was to become women who direct their own destiny, rather than suffer it. I don't know how I could present this better to you."
"How long did the training at the Neon Nights last?" the cop asked.
"Several years."
"And could you leave the institution in the meantime?"

"What kind of question is that? What do you think? I lived here in the city, had my own apartment; do you think I was in need of some dormitory? But I see you misunderstand. The Neon Nights was not some high school. The lucky ones who were allowed to enter the realm of glamour went there after school and on weekends."
I knew I should have eaten less in the morning, because a bit of vomit came up. I wiped my mouth discreetly. My ears didn't really want to take in what they heard.

"Anyway, they took the studies very seriously. They only allowed a good grade in three subjects; in everything else, you had to perform excellently, otherwise you couldn't continue the training. They motivated us this way to put as much as possible into everything. There was no such thing as something being difficult. They taught us to fight."
"And were there those who dropped out during the training programs?" the colleague pried further.
"There are always such. Of course there were here too."
"And what became of their fate?"
"What would have become? Nothing. Or as I know, they had to repay the scholarship. But that was all."
"And what kind of sum could it be?"
"Ugh," the girl shook herself. "I don't know. It never seemed that this sum interested anyone. I was in no danger of having to return it, and of course neither was my father. I want to allude..."
"We understand what you allude to, don't worry," the detective took back the initiative. "What age girls did they deal with there?"
"High schoolers. That's why they admitted me when I started secondary school."
"Do you keep in touch with anyone from the Neon Nights, by any chance?"
"Of course I do. That too was an important point of the training, that we learned to value our connections."
"Would others also like to testify? Or just tell their experiences?"
"Definitely. We would like the truth about Edgar to come out as soon as possible. I don't know on what basis they formulated these charges against him. But I can assure you they are ridiculous."
"So you didn't have bad experiences regarding the Neon Nights?"
"None at all. Of course, there were a few exercises that some might have felt were difficult, but I don't think one should complain because of that."
"What do you mean?"
I waited curiously to see what would come of this, and how the lie this girl came here with would fit the difficult exercises she mentioned.

"As I said, the most successful people taught us in their respective fields, and successful people are sometimes difficult of nature. Here too, someone might have felt they were behaved with humiliatingly."
"What is to be understood by that?"
"Sometimes we were scolded if something didn't go the way it should have."
"Were you verbally abused?"
"Abused?" the girl was puzzled. "What kind of word is that? They just shouted at us, a few cried, that's all that happened. Afterward, we wanted success even more."
"And were you not physically abused?"
"Again this abuse. This is some fetish of yours," the witness established. "There was a time when someone was slapped. But this really fit in."
"You said you were made to sign a non-disclosure. Why was that needed?"

"I think it's pretty clear. To preserve the exclusivity of the training. The girls were admitted to the training courses from a well-defined circle. And this circle was obviously not the song circle of folk cultivators from Pettyville. They didn't want some competitors to notice the training here. This segment of education targets a very small market. Every piece of information is behind the scenes, if I may say so."
"Do you know of any case when someone was sexually exploited or perhaps abused?"
"No. And I can firmly state that nothing of the sort happened either. Despite certain types of training touching upon this area too, of course in a discrete environment."
"What do you mean by that?" the detective asked.
"That no, such things didn't happen. How a woman gets to know her body, I think, doesn't belong to the category of sexual abuse. Much rather biology."
"I see, I understood, thank you," the detective closed it. "Is there anything else you would say?"

"No, there isn't," the girl replied. "Perhaps only that I hope this case is closed as soon as possible. What one hears on TV is truly unpleasant. I don't know who it could come from, but every word of it is a lie."

It was good that a glass wall separated me from her, because I would have liked most to tear her apart. I was incredibly angry. Tears were close. In front of Matt, however, I still couldn't afford this behavior. I couldn't place what the girl was talking about. I only felt she breezed in here in her multi-thousand-dollar outfit, and with such ease twisted reality as if it had never existed.
colors: white
cold blue
gold

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-One
paragraphs: March 10, 2022
I wasn't in a good mood. I had no problem with the gloomy weather, but even more so because it reflected my mood.

"She sat there like some kind of prima donna, pretending that it was New York and that she was a good friend of the president. Specifically, I threw up," I explained to Anton, with whom I couldn't talk about what happened last night, because he went alone to a reception, which I told him back in time.
"Do you know what keeps coming to my mind?" he asked with a beginning enthusiasm in his voice.
"I'm afraid I do. Do we have three thousand dollars?"

"I know we have it," he smiled, "I just don't know if we want to spend it. But I feel more and more that those articles know something. That's where we first read about the Neon Nights in a completely different context. What if they write something about these training programs in them too?"

I couldn't help but agree with Anton, though I tried not to. Not because I too wanted to parade in a multi-thousand-dollar outfit in the lobby of the prosecutor's office—I could have lived with it, I must add—but because I didn't want to accept that an aspect of this soul-destroying organization existed that facilitated the self-fulfillment of rich girls on the ruins of our dreams.

But life is just like that: it doesn't really pay attention to what we pray for, it is only interested in the rock-hard reality. And in that reality, the Neon Nights could easily have created a front organization with which it erased the traces of our exploitation, and of course sent the beautiful children of well-paying, loving fathers in our stead to where they belonged. To the top of the world.
Were the articles for which we ended up leaving four thousand dollars useful? Undoubtedly yes, even if it was hard for me to utter a single good word during the entire ride home.
"Four thousand dollars for this spit in the face?!" I protested.
"At least we have proof of this too now. By the way, where the hell could these letters have been published? They seem more like e-mails than newspaper articles," Anton noted.

"Because they are. Newsletters in printed form. The whole thing is quite a fancy piece of shit. Acting classes, singing classes, supermodel course... And do you know what hurts the most in all this?" I asked rhetorically, if that's even the right expression. "That it really worked out for these girls. As a little girl, I dreamed of this too. Then reality slapped me in the face."

I was sad. I wanted to cry, which I could have done with Anton, but I felt that the situation would not allow it. I couldn't feel sorry for myself, because that would have offended the prosecutor Amanda Evans, and she didn't deserve to have her accomplishments dismissed because of childhood dreams. You're one hell of a tough girl, Amy! I told myself.
"I think so too," Anton agreed. It seemed I had spoken out loud again.

The days passed and Liz Bennet's girlfriends also joined the president's praise club with their confessions. In the meantime, it turned out that the girl's name is Liz Bennet. If I want to be precise, it wasn't about finding out, because the police already knew who she was, but I didn't remember her name, I was so angry with her.

One day, I really had to stay late. In response to the new information, we had to work out another strategy, which took a lot of time. The president's team worked to paint the complaint as the accusations of offended, dismissed girls, and the explanations in the articles appearing in the media sometimes supported this quite believably. I got home exhausted and tired. It was already past midnight.

On the street, the lights were unusually dim. I wanted nothing but a shower and to get to bed as soon as possible. The house was not locked. A bad feeling filled me. It was always important to Anton that the door should not remain open. During the day I sometimes argued with him because of this. Nevertheless, it obviously occurred that the door remained so for some reason.

The apartment was quiet; I took off my shoes in the hallway in silence so as not to wake Anton with the knocking. As soon as I entered the living room, the shape of a figure sitting in an armchair emerged in the dim light.
"Have you come?" Anton asked.
"I have. What is this, some interrogation?" I inquired.
"If I guess correctly, a policeman should be standing out there somewhere, shouldn't he?" How could he have realized?

So I really came home to an interrogation. My whole life I hated such things. I detested being called on the carpet by anyone, and since I started working, I had even less patience for such situations. I found it slightly strange, because Anton never created a situation to make this obvious. This sitting in the armchair in the dark, however, turned out to be quite theatrical.
"Why the hell aren't you sleeping yet?" I retorted, and with that momentum I turned on the light. At that moment, a quiet gasp escaped from me.

In the middle of the living room lay the body of an unknown man face down, facing towards the bedroom, with a silenced pistol lying next to him. A pool of blood spread under the man, reflecting the nearby furniture. Between the hall and the living room, a smaller but all the more visible blood smear stretched along for about two meters until it ended at the edge of the carpet. Anton was sitting in his armchair facing the hall, holding a revolving Colt Python in his right hand and Mr. Fuzzy's lifeless bloody body in his left. There was emptiness in his eyes, disappointment in his voice.
"You could have let me know," he noted.
"What happened here?" I asked.

"You are the specialist," he answered. "This bastard obviously broke in, and I woke up to it; the cat started moving in the meantime, so the guy shot him, then headed toward our room, from where I shot him. This is self-defense, isn't it?"
"It is."
"My God, Amy! Tell me it's self-defense, right?" His voice trembled.
"To be precise, it's justifiable self-defense, but based on what you've said, yes, it was."
"I'm going to get quite used to this," he noted.
"What the hell happened here, Anton?" I asked again, but this question was really asking: how could this have happened?
"I thought you would be the one to give the answer to that," he put the gun down on the floor. He stroked his dead cat with both hands.
"I'm the one who's supposed to know?" I asked, bewildered.
"I was hoping you knew, yes. Say, Amy, wasn't there supposed to be a policeman out there?" he asked again.
"Yes, there should have been," I admitted. "And I'm going to find out where the hell he was."
"Why did we need a policeman stationed in front of our house, Amy? Shouldn't I have known about this? Did you know we were in danger?"
"Does it matter?"
"Be honest with me! Have you been threatened, Amy?" he asked, agitated.
"Right after Jess's death," I replied.
"You must be fucking kidding me. That was over a month ago! Why the fuck couldn't you tell me you were threatened?"
"Watch your mouth!" I snapped. I couldn't stand it when he swore, even if he had every right to.
"For fuck's sake, Amy, why didn't you tell me?"
"Don't you dare say that word again! Do you think you're being tough right now?" I shouted at him. "Watch your language, or we're not talking!"

I was incredibly angry. Not at Anton. Least of all at him, but I didn't want his foul language to make me angry at him, too. I was mostly angry at myself. He was completely right. I should have told him, but I hadn't wanted to. I thought I could protect him. A policeman had been guarding us for weeks, but I had wanted to keep it a secret from him. When I looked at him, I hadn't seen a man who was worried, only how little he ate each day. He had no appetite. And I had no strength left to worry about that on top of the investigation. I thought I had everything under control. I was wrong.
"Why couldn't you tell me?" Anton asked. "Shouldn't I have known we were in danger?"
"Do you know how little you've been eating since this all started?" I attacked him. "Even less after Jess's death. I'm really worried about you."
"This is such nonsense," he grumbled. "I'm not a toddler you have to sit next to constantly."
"But you are very sensitive," I switched to a calmer tone, and sat on the arm of the chair. "I thought I could keep things under control."
"This is so pathetic," he looked in front of him. "Do you really think I'm that pathetic, Amy?"
"No way!" I answered. "How can someone who kills an assassin be pathetic?" I looked at the corpse. I was honestly proud of Anton. "I should have let you in on this."
"Maybe not after all," he continued after a pause. "Maybe it was better that way. They say better safe than sorry, but I would have hated to wait months for that to happen."

"You were very brave!" I complimented him, and I really meant it, despite how silly it sounded in this situation. "My God, Anton! They tried to have me killed by a hitman!" the realization hit me. It was as if the adrenaline from the initial shock was only now letting me think clearly. Suddenly, a gripping fear overtook me. "I have to call the cop!"
"Where the hell have you been?!"
"Don't you start with me...!"
"They attacked my fiance in my own house!"
"Call forensics, someone is dead. I'm calling the inspector!"

When I managed to think through what had happened, I felt helpless. It was terrible to think that a hitman broke into our house and tried to kill Anton. I thought control had irrecoverably slipped from my hands, and I had to admit that I couldn't take responsibility for those I love.

Jess's death was a huge loss, but I had to draw strength from it and work on. The move against Anton, however, was already aimed at breaking me, in which I felt they had achieved success. Anton wouldn't have been a martyr, but rather the clear failure of my struggle for justice. A loss I couldn't explain in any other way than that I am unfit for the task.

Anton, however, warded off the attack. From his perspective, only situational self-defense mattered, and I hated myself for not being able to leave it at that, although with all my heart this would have been the only thing that interested me. If I had come home today to find Anton lying in a pool of blood in the middle of the living room instead of the hitman, it's very possible that I would have turned the Colt on myself. I felt I couldn't be grateful enough to him for saving both our lives.

When he spoke to the crime scene investigators, he behaved as if he were on a movie set. I imagined him choreographing the scene perfectly, then having the actors play it out. The situation was pretty clear. It happened a few minutes after eleven. From Anton's gestures, it came alive before my eyes how the hitman slips in, how the cat gets scared, and how Anton steps out of the bedroom door with his revolver, then shoots. If the guy hadn't shot the cat, Anton would perhaps have thought I had come home. Too terrifying to contemplate. Mr. Fuzzy's misfortune, however, became our luck.

After the forensics and Anton's statement, I felt I couldn't stay in the house. This also had to do with the police not being done with the cleanup, and I didn't want to sleep in a place where a dead man's blood had coagulated into a pool in the middle of the living room. We decided to spend the night in a hotel.
"We haven't been to a hotel in a long time," Anton commented as we lay on the bed.
"We haven't had time to travel lately."
"We could stay in a hotel in the city sometimes," he suggested.
"It's not customary to go to a hotel where you live."
"People really could. You don't even have to leave the hotel. It works anywhere. Like here and now," Anton suggested.

"I guess we've already done it, then," I answered. "I don't think I'd want to leave here until morning anyway." We looked at each other. I just realized that we hadn't even looked at each other since I turned on the light and the image of our ravaged living room unfolded before me. He smiled, but there was sadness in his eyes. We were both very tired. "I'm so sorry about your cat," I continued.
"If he hadn't misled the hitman," he said, "the situation might be different now."
"I haven't been able to get that possibility out of my head since I watched you tell the police what happened."
"Everything is fine," he reassured me. "It was exciting."
"No kidding!"
"You know, I noticed that he was fiddling with the lock a lot," he continued. "At first I thought maybe you'd had a few drinks and couldn't find your key."
"Excuse me, but the very assumption is offensive!" I smiled. "So you were awake?"
"I wake up to even the slightest noise," he answered. "I thought it was strange from the start. After he came in, I didn't hear him take off his shoes, which you always do."
"Am I that predictable?" I asked.
"You did exactly the same today when you arrived."
"Because I do. I don't want to wake you up," I said, caressing his face.
"I always wake up. I can't sleep soundly until you're home."

He slid gently closer on the bed and kissed my lips. We put our foreheads together. We slept like this many times, when in the middle of our night conversations we suddenly got sleepy. Both of us closed our eyes, and we only heard each other's breathing. It felt good to lie like this. We held each other's hand, and snuggled very closely. Anton always put one hand on my thigh at times like this, and swallowed hard a few times, which we both heard ridiculously loudly in this meditative silence.

Of course I knew that despite his pretenses, he actually had no intention of sleeping, which became clear from his next movements. chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Two
paragraphs: March 17, 2022

News of the attack quickly swept through the media. I didn't mind it. The power of publicity, I hoped, might protect us. The president assured us of his sympathy—me, the woman representing the state in the trial of the century—and condemned the intimidation. Of course, I didn't believe a word of it, but he presented it so convincingly that if I hadn't known him, I would have thought this hypocritical charade was genuine concern.

The investigation continued, and as a result of the attack, the patrols surrounded us even more. They offered us a safe house in the city center, but we didn't accept it. I felt that if I couldn't come home to my usual environment and at least pretend for a little bit that everything was fine, I would go crazy. We lived under the constant supervision of four patrol cars, which had the advantage that no matter where we went, we didn't have to bother with our own car; in fact, if we really wanted to, they even turned on the flashing lights, although to be honest, the officers got tired of crawling through the city traffic earlier than I did.
One day, Matt unexpectedly showed up in my office.
"We have him," he said matter-of-factly.
"Who?"
"Ross Wilson is back."
"Only now?" I asked.
"What do you mean, 'only now'?"
"Let me ask it differently, then. Why now? Where did they dig him up?"

"Toby McRae called two days ago to say he had tracked him down. Ever since he visited us, he's been completely immersed in Wilson's old affairs. He found a lot of oddities. He didn't just cover up Neon Nights business, but he also popped up in other cases where something had to be swept under the rug for businesses connected to the president."
"And is he here in town?"
"According to McRae, yes."
"Do you know where, Matt?"
"He just sent over the address," he answered.

I became as excited as a first-grader going to school for the first time. This lead came completely unexpectedly, and it was still hot, as if it had just been pulled from the oven. I wanted to see this man. I wanted to meet him and question him about every case where we assumed the investigation had been closed prematurely because of him.

Within moments we were speeding through the streets, sirens blaring, with a patrol car close behind. Wilson was spotted this morning at a hotel in the Nouveau Palais district, so we had every reason to believe we could catch him. The informant McRae was in contact with hadn't seen Wilson leave the building.

Terror filled the receptionist's eyes when he saw the three uniformed policemen with their hands on their holsters in the hotel lobby. It was a modern, sleek building, much more ordinary than, say, the Corinthia Royal in an upscale district of the city center.
"Which is Ross Wilson's room?" I asked, as he nervously began to search the register.
"Room 39," he replied.
"Is he alone?"
"I don't know. Guests don't have to check in their visitors."
"Then how do you know if someone is freeloading?"
"They pay for the room," the receptionist said defensively.

Matt and I went toward the elevator, and the other two officers approached the room through the stairwell. The hallway was completely empty. Skylights illuminated the level; the corridor was bathed in a true flood of light.
"Police!" one of the patrolmen knocked on the door, but there was no answer from inside. He repeated it.

"Stand back!" said the other, kicking the door open. The lock flew out of place as if it had never been there. I grunted appreciatively, though it was disconcerting to see how little protection it offered against a break-in.

The two patrolmen went ahead and secured the apartment, which consisted of only three rooms including the bath. Their effort, though undoubtedly professional, proved unnecessary, because a sizable chunk was missing from the skull of the lifeless body sitting at the table. Despite seeing a similar corpse in the middle of my living room two days ago, I almost threw up.
"Dead," remarked one of the patrolmen.
"Are you sure?" I quipped. "Blood" had splattered up to the ceiling.
"Is it him?" I asked Matt, who was already calling Toby McRae for identification.
Twenty minutes later, the forensics team was already searching room 39.
"Ma'am!" one of them said. "We found the number of the man who attacked you on Wilson's phone."
"What?" I asked, taken aback. "Did Wilson hire that man?"
"They spoke ten days ago, it's possible."
"Trace every single number! He must have spoken to someone else. There's no way this was his own idea."
"We'll look into it," he reassured me.

A true storm of emotions raged inside me. An hour ago, I was still fantasizing about how I would question Wilson about his dark dealings, yet now I was brooding over why he would be the one to hire someone to attempt on Anton's life. I didn't feel safe at all anymore; even with patrols constantly in my wake, the world could change completely in just a few hours. The whole case was beginning to resemble a mafia movie where you stumble over corpses at every turn. I hated all of it. Since the attack, Anton slept with a pistol under his pillow, and the lights in the living room were kept on constantly. The image of Wilson's blown-apart skull was burned into my brain, and only one thought kept running through my head: who could be capable of shooting a man in the head in cold blood, like some butcher.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Three
paragraphs: March 25, 2022
"How did you sleep?" I asked Anton around nine in the morning, when I finally dragged myself out of bed.

I woke up to the smell of sunny-side-up eggs. Lately, the dividing line between the weekend and the weekday had slipped a bit. Sometimes I was in the office on a Sunday, other times I was at home at odd hours. I didn't plan anything for this morning either, I only wanted to go to the prosecutor's office around noon.
"I didn't sleep," he answered, although it didn't show on him at first glance.
"I didn't even notice," I remarked. "Why not?"
"My mind was racing about Jake Cooper the whole time. Then, around three, I went to the study to write instead."
"Is that when inspiration hit you?" I asked, puzzled. "Are you crazy? Why didn't you wake me up? I might have been able to help."
"No, no," he protested. "I was glad you were finally resting, and I had to think everything through."
Anton looked uneasy. I began to worry that he had figured out something terrible.
"I don't know if I'm right," he began. "So you shouldn't take it as gospel."
"I won't," I reassured him.

"I couldn't get it through my head why Cooper is important. We only know a few things about him. One is that he recruited you, the other is that he was there when Mike Alioglu died. We also know that he lived in the Liberty district, and we know where. But we don't know who he lived with. Mrs. Alioglu didn't know his parents."
"Yes, that's true," I answered.
"Since then, however, there has been no information about him."
"Yes," I agreed again.
"But then why did Jess give the detectives his name? If he was only involved in those two things, why do we need to speak with him?"
"Forgive me, but isn't it enough that we ended up there because of him?" I protested indignantly.

"Enough," he answered, "but you said you never saw Cooper again after he brought you guys to Neon Nights. He never became a gentleman. He vanished. Then what could he have known about how the club operated? How could he have helped? Why did Jess give the detectives his name?"
"I don't know," I answered, and it started to bother me. Anton was right. If you put it that way, it really wasn't clear why Jake Cooper was on the list alongside Hermione and David King.
"So I had to put things in a new light," he explained. "Either Jessica was just hoping they'd find Jake and he'd know something, or she was sure we'd benefit from finding him."
"Knowing Jessica, it was definitely the second option," I answered. "She knew what she was doing."
"In that case, she also knew why we needed Jake Cooper. What if Jake did a lot more than what we've associated with him so far?"
"What are you thinking?" I asked Anton.
"Let's say he dropped a threatening letter into Jessica's mailbox."
"Do you think Jess knew it was him?"
"She might have suspected it, yes. And I'm saying he could have killed Jessica, too," Anton suggested.
"Maybe Jake showed up already in the fall? Is that why Jess decided to leave messages with the lawyer?"
"Why not? Even more than that. I think Jake Cooper is a member of Neon Nights, and always was, whether you saw him there or not."
"Is that what occurred to you last night?"
"Yes," he answered firmly.
"You really know how to shuffle the deck," I said, "but I'm afraid reality isn't a book where the details only fit a pre-determined path. Even if it were, Cooper is still nowhere to be found."
"Yes, but I have another theory."
"What theory?" I asked, sensing that Anton was hesitant to share it with me for some reason. "Spill it, Sherlock, what did you write?"

I had sensed correctly that he was afraid to tell me; he himself didn't want to believe what he had come up with. A few minutes later, I understood why. The world spun around me. What he said seemed completely impossible, yet it was a sound argument in every detail. I turned it over in my mind again and again, trying to find a flaw in it, but for some reason, I couldn't.
"It's a little scary that you can't find any flaws in it," Anton noted. "I was hoping you'd point out what I failed to take into account."
"You failed to consider a lot of things, honey," I answered. "The only problem is, that only made it all the more factual."
Anton's idea really upset me. I felt like I was going to go crazy if I didn't follow up on things right away.
"Will you come with me?" I asked.
"I'll gladly drive you, but you won't get much use out of me," he said apologetically. "My mind is completely blank."
"That's fine, it will do anyway."

Water stood in puddles in front of the single-story house in the Liberty district. It had been raining continuously for a week, and the drains had been overwhelmed for days. The street was empty, save for a few muddy dogs wandering about with their soaked fur. Even though it was noon, the fog made it almost impossible to see anything without headlights. The old garden furniture sat like an eyesore among the ruins of the front yard, and except for one thing, everything was just as it had been when I visited with the detectives: a faint light was glowing in the window. Excitement flooded my entire body.
"He is home," I noted, and slid my gun from the glove compartment into my holster.
"Shouldn't I go too?" Anton asked.
"No, you stay in the car! Call Wilbur and Matt! Tell them Cooper is back!"

As I approached the door, my heart was hammering in my chest. I was used to doing field work, but I had never raided anyone on my own. For a second, I even surprised myself by being here, but then my hand automatically turned the doorknob.
"What the hell are you doing here?!" Jeff yelled at me from his laptop.
"I could ask you the same thing," I countered. "Shouldn't you be mourning Jessica somewhere in Montaukville?"
"My father recovered, and I had business in the city," he answered. "What are you doing here?"
"As far as I know, you don't live here," I pressed. "Or is the apartment in the Gemini Residential Park just a cover?"
"Not that it's any of your business, but I sold it," he replied. "I couldn't live there alone."
"Already? You have a pretty good realtor, as a matter of fact."
"I'm asking for the last time, Miss Evans, what are you doing here?"
"Jake Cooper. Or is this house not his?"

"Jake is not home right now," he replied, rather perplexingly. "But this was already the third question that I didn't even want to answer, while you actually didn't answer one. How did you know I was here?"
"You're pretty clumsy if I could interrogate you like that against your will, aren't you? Anyway, that was your first sensible question, Jefferson."
"And are you going to answer too, or did you just come to insult me?"

"Actually, you surprise me. I expected you to be here, but your reaction is completely different from what I anticipated. You should know that I'm investigating Jake, and that I would find this house sooner or later. Why isn't it bothering you more that I'm not surprised to see you here?"
"Everything bothers me," he replied, as if he didn't want to understand what I said.
"By the way, where is Jake?" I goaded.
"He'll be here."
"When did he leave?"
"Not so long ago."
"Do you think I should wait for him?"
"If I were you, I wouldn't risk it."
"Why not?"
"Jake is not a very kind person, and especially not with you."
"Not that you are one, Jefferson."
"I don't know why that surprises you."
"You misunderstand. I'm not surprised."

Ever since Mrs. Alioglu pressed Mike's picture into my hand, I kept it in my wallet. I didn't know if I was ever going to meet Jake, but I thought that if life brought me to it, I would grant the poor woman's request.
"There is a guy here who, I think, might have had something to do with Jake. But correct me if I'm wrong."
"Who is it?" he asked.
I gave him Mike's photo.
"Where did you get this?" he asked perhaps his second sensible question since I had been there.
"So you know him?"
"He's Mike Alioglu, Evans, not Jake."
"Of course he is," I replied contentedly. "But he was Jake's friend, if I'm not mistaken."
Jeff buried his curly head in his hands. By the time he looked up, his gaze had completely changed.

"I didn't say you were wrong," he agreed. "He couldn't have been Jeff's friend. He hardly knew him. Jeff was still very young when Mike died." As strange as it sounded, I knew he was telling the truth.
"I'm glad we finally meet, Jake!" I greeted him. "I see you've come home."
"So, how does this work? Is it even fitting for me to ask such a thing?"
"You can ask whatever you want," he replied coldly. "When did you realize?"
"Unfortunately it wasn't I who realized, but Anton."
"Your husband?!" he laughed. "The one who came with you to Montaukville? He seemed far too simple to have ideas like that."
"He is not my husband, but obviously that doesn't matter at all. Are there more of you?"
Jake stared into my eyes.
"Why? Aren't two personalities enough?"
"If you ask me, it's one too many."

"You say this as if you knew either of us. By the way, Jeff was right: I'm not happy you're here, and you'd better make it short, because although it might be surprising, I am not the poster child of patience."
"Don't think I want to drag it out. You only have to answer a few questions," I reassured him, and meanwhile I was wondering when Wilbur and Matt would finally get here.
"What are you curious about?"
"Do you have a doctor?"
"You want to start that far back? I thought you needed information for the investigation."
"That's part of it too, but if you don't want to answer, well, don't answer."
Jake nodded in agreement.
"Did you kill Jessica?" I asked, shifting to something more current.
"I didn't think you had such a good technique. Do many suspects crack?" he bantered. "It would be too simple to answer no. I'd rather say: I don't know."
"Yeah, I thought it wouldn't make any sense. I'd rather tell you what I think, okay?"
"As you wish, then get the hell out of here."
"Let's not get ahead of ourselves," I answered.

Jake seemed very confident, but I didn't understand why. He had to know that since we finally have him, I won't be satisfied with listening to his flippant answers. However, all signs indicated that he hadn't realized this.
"Don't think you have the upper hand, Jake," I began. "In fact, I want you to know that you're in a very bad spot. You are my number one suspect in Jessica's murder."
Jake stared blankly before him; it didn't seem he took what I said too much to heart.
"I thought we were attacked. But you obviously know better," he replied.

"Furthermore, we know that the investigation into Mike's case was closed prematurely thanks to Ross Wilson. So the killer was never caught. Do you know who the suspect was before that?" He didn't reply. "You, Jake. And perhaps not without reason. What do you think about that?"
"I think nothing of it. And I think you forget something quite important."
"What would that be?" I asked back, because I was sure he only wanted to scare me.

"I'm actually surprised at how clueless you are about what I know about you. You somehow assume that everyone sees you as just a simple prosecutor. Of course, I understand why you think that. You really managed to hide everything about your past life well. You can take this as a compliment, and you can even thank Jessica that she never let anything slip. And believe me, I tried to get it out of her."

His unexpected threat made me sick. I guessed where he wanted to go, but I didn't understand why he confessed that he didn't have anything. If he hadn't, all I could think about was when he would pull something out of the sleeve to corner me.

"But that doesn't mean I don't know your name, Alice Bucks. I know exactly who you are. In fact, I remember you. I've followed your entire career in whore-training, don't worry. Unlike you, I remember everything, and I can say one thing. No matter how much you tried to avoid it, the world is going to find out about you."

I tried to remain calm, but only managed to freeze my face expressionless. Inside, it affected me just as he intended. Let him rot, I thought to myself. I knew Jess kept silent about me; she swore to this back when I presented to her what I would do with my past, but I wasn't prepared for a person whom I believed had permanently disappeared to still address me as Alice today. I hated the knowledge that he knows me; I felt transparent, as if not only was I naked, but my soul was completely vulnerable too. Of course, it would have been too early to despair. My incognito rested on rock-solid foundations, and Jake couldn't possess evidence against me. Regardless, I knew he would expose the truth, and I must be such an actress as only Jess could be. Seriously. How could she hide Jake from me?

I didn't answer Cooper's threats, I just smiled when I heard Wilbur's heavy footsteps in the puddles. Take him in, boys, I ordered as soon as the door opened, and run him through that spiel about his rights.
Anton, sitting in the car, didn't even dare to budge; he kept staring at the window of the house, as if anything essential could be seen from outside.
"So, how was it?" he asked.
"It was quite terrifying," I answered. "I have no idea how Jessica could live with him."
"It seems she loved him."
"And this I understand even less," for a moment I wondered what kind of relationship they shared in that strange threesome.
"Did anything come out?"
"Besides the dissociative identity disorder?"
"Yeah."
"Not about the murders."
"And about anything else?"
"Everything about Alice Bucks that wasn't supposed to."

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Four
paragraphs: March 25, 2022

On the way to the station, I racked my brains over how we were going to get Jake to talk. In the morning, I hadn't really been prepared for the encounter, so I didn't know what to ask him and failed to ask the right questions. Weeks earlier, it would have been easy. Today, the confrontation had come too suddenly. Regardless, I was satisfied with the result. We had finally found Jake Cooper, and he couldn't have been more deeply involved in the events. Jeff and Jake were the same person. This development sent chills down my spine, and my every muscle spasmed. I was shivering in my seat like one does on cold winter evenings without a coat on a bistro terrace, where they seem to think a thin blanket solves everything.

But now, no matter how many blankets I could have wrapped around myself, the shivering came from within, uncontrollably. I tried to run through the questions: Did he kill Jessica? Did he drop the threats into the mailbox? Did he send the hitman and kill Wilson? What did he do after he recruited us? And of course, what really happened to Mike Alioglu? I knew he wouldn't answer if I was the one asking. I wouldn't have been able to get Jeff to talk, let alone Jake. Of course, I wasn't the one who had to interrogate him. We had professionals for that, who did their jobs excellently.

Beyond this, I was genuinely curious about Jake and Jeff's mental state, though I didn't even know if I should be thinking such things. Which one was dominant? Which one existed first? Going by the old stories, it was Jake. Perhaps Jeff was born out of his love for Jessica, which inevitably brought to mind the origin myth of some Greek deity. Of course, I wasn't motivated by sympathy or concern; I didn't want to understand his problems, and I didn't believe his illness could absolve him of his actions. It was just my prosecutor self wanting to get inside his head. I was interested in it purely as a case.

Anton followed the officers without a word; I could tell he preferred not to be in the way. As soon as he heard that Alice Bucks's cover was blown, he grew anxious, but I cut him off before he could get worked up. I didn't want to deal with Alice just yet. I knew exactly what Jake had on her: nothing.

The cars stopped in the police courtyard, and Jake, led in handcuffs, was taken to the interrogation room. He said nothing, marching silently in the ring of officers. In the car, he had called his lawyer, whom we barely had to wait for. He was a well-dressed, tall man with a stern gaze. I had never seen anyone quite like him before. His entire presence demanded respect and radiated a frosty atmosphere.

Where could Jeff have found him, I wondered. As a prosecutor, you know the city's best-known defense attorneys, yet he wasn't familiar. This was despite the fact that he was clearly one of the stars of his profession.
"You have to release him today," he declared with a straight face. The declarative tone added even more weight to his words.
"We won't," I replied, and tried to remain as calm as I could.

I was deeply outraged. As if it weren't enough that the suspect refused to talk, now this lawyer had only come to obstruct our work. He could defend him for all I cared, but without an interrogation, bringing him here was completely in vain.
"We can't let him go until he's spoken."
"He is under medical treatment," he replied.
"What was he doing in the Liberty district, then?"

A lot depends on this trial. Public trust in power could be shaken. The Russians are at war, the Arab world is seething. They are attacking the president himself. Doesn't this country need peace and security?"
Wittmann made a real speech. He genuinely believed that what he had to say had a great impact on me.
"You don't believe in the president's guilt?" I asked. "But we have clear evidence against him."

"Evidence," he said the word with a pitying edge. "What can't be proven in today's world? They will also accept that you are Alice Bucks. I assure you that the moment that is proven, you will be kicked out of the prosecutor's office so fast your feet won't touch the ground. But even if by some chance it isn't true, you must see for yourself what a filthy world we live in, where everyone who doesn't dance to their tune is discredited."
"Who wants them to?" I asked. "Who are you talking about?"
To this Attorney General Murphy Wittmann answered with a mock smile, and I still didn't understand whom he meant by this.
"Until the trial is over, I'm taking Wright's place. You will report to me, and I will issue the instructions. And you will carry them out, is that understood?"
I didn't want to think at length about the offer, since I knew whatever he said, I would go my own way as long as I could.
"Understood," I answered.

"Personally, I'm sure Wright used her position to force her views on you. I'm not angry with you," he added defensively. "You're just an impressionable girl. I just want the president to get a fair trial."
"I understand, sir," I answered. "In that case, if there's nothing else, I..." and with that, I closed the door of Wright's office from the outside.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Six
paragraphs: April 11, 2022

Several journalists were loitering in front of the prosecutor's office. Like vultures, they hunted for any exciting bit of information about the case. Our press officers did their best to answer the most important questions, but naturally, many went unanswered.

I was feeling nauseous. It wasn't because of the journalists waiting outside; rather, it was Murphy Wittmann's outrageously despicable move that had thrown me. Murphy Wittmann. How familiar that name must have sounded among the students of the high school where Edgar Mortenstein and Wittmann had gone decades ago. I knew the Chief Prosecutor owed his position to this connection, but for some reason, I had lived in a fantasy world where Athena Wright's presence commanded respect and provided security against such obvious abuses. If anything, Wittmann would have been justified in putting me in my place for this naivety, but that wasn't why he did it.

I stood at a loss in the corridor. I didn't know what to do. Then, guided by a sudden idea, I caught myself and went out in front of the prosecutor's office, straight into the arms of the reporters who wanted me. I didn't have time to think about the consequences. I didn't even want to. At first, I saw complete confusion on their faces. They hadn't known anything about me for days. I came by bus and had even entered the building with sunglasses and a scarf covering myself. But now I stood in front of them from head to toe, because I thought that from now on it would be better to do everything as publicly as possible.
"Are you really a whore?" asked a young guy who thought it was cool to start like that.
"Just like your mother," answered an older journalist. Those standing around welcomed his response with appreciation.
"Are you Alice Bucks?" another inquired.
"No, I am Amanda Evans, and I have nothing to do with the one they are talking about."
"Then why does the president claim this?"
"You'd have to ask him that. But I know exactly why he claims I am Alice."
"And why?" several asked immediately.

Excitement buzzed around the site of the impromptu press conference. When people inside saw me talking to the reporters, several rushed out to stop me, but I ignored them. I wanted to take matters into my own hands.

"It's because Alice Bucks was indeed held captive in the Neon Nights, then after they sold her to Marlo Martinez, she too fell victim during the Martinez settlement. And the president wants to conflate me with her because he thinks he can get me out of his way by this."
"Did you know Alice Bucks?"
Before the law, what I was saying might have seemed like a lie, but my conscience was clean when I answered.
"Yes, I knew her, but I am not Alice Bucks."
"And how did you know her?"
"I got to know her at Marlo Martinez's."
"Were you also a member of the Martinez clan?"
"No, I was not a member."
"Then?"
A shocked silence followed.
"I grew up in a children's home, just like Alice," I continued. "Then, at the age of fifteen, I ended up in Marlo Martinez's circle."
"Then you are indeed a whore?" asked the guy again. I didn't know from which paper he arrived, but for some reason he tried very hard to remain memorable.
"I was in Martinez's employ as a maid."
"And doesn't this count as a disqualifying reason to be a prosecutor in this case?" another journalist asked.
"That I knew Alice Bucks?" I asked back.
"Yes. Perhaps you have a personal stake in seeing the president behind bars?"

"I think it's hard for anyone to remain emotionally detached from such atrocities. In that sense, I suppose you could say that. But no. I have no personal interest in this. I only want to bring justice to those who turned to the state with their grievances."
"Don't you think that in the current situation it is dangerous to weaken presidential power?"

"I want it to be clear to everyone that Edgar Mortenstein is not synonymous with the presidency. The fact that he occupies this office does not diminish public trust in the presidency itself. On the contrary, the judiciary strengthens that authority when it helps remove those who abuse it or are unfit for it. Of course, whether Edgar Mortenstein is indeed unfit for this office is for the court to decide."
"Did your boyfriend really get disappointed in you?" chimed in another 'excellent' journalist.

"What kind of question is that? Do you think I'm causing disappointment by fighting for the truth, or by standing out here alone in front of the press? What does my boyfriend have to do with any of this? Did you honestly feel it was absolutely necessary to ask that?"
"When will you hold an official press conference?" several asked, to which I replied only after a few seconds.

"More official than this? I won't. We'd better get used to keeping the press informed about the status of the case. Up until now, we may have been too guarded with our words and worried that information would get out that would hinder the investigation. However, the reality is that this matter is everyone's business. We will not hide any more, and please, whatever questions you have, ask them to my colleagues, whom I instruct to answer everything they can, keeping in mind the interests of the investigation."
"Did something happen that made you suddenly change your strategy?" one of them inquired.
"Yes," I replied immediately.
"And what was it?"
"I just learned that District Attorney Athena Wright was removed from her position by Chief Prosecutor Murphy Wittmann."
"When did this happen?"
"Probably sometime yesterday."
"And what justified this change?"
"I'd be more than happy to answer that for you."
Suddenly a window was flung open, from where the Chief Prosecutor's shouting was heard.
"Evans! What did I tell you? You will do as I say!"
At this, the journalists began to grow curious.
"Did Murphy Wittmann forbid you from making statements?"

"We didn't discuss that. He only told me that Wright is a man-hating lesbian who went on a rampage against male leaders, and cited several recent cases where, thanks to Wright, men in senior positions—mostly accused of sexual abuse—went to prison. You might recall that the president spoke about similar matters in his last speech, in which he tried to conflate me with Alice Bucks."
"By this do you want to say that Wittmann replaced Wright at the president's instruction?"
"You can obviously see the connection for yourself if you want to," I answered.
"Can you prove this?"
"Only indirectly. However, it is well known to everyone that they were not only schoolmates, but are still good friends to this day. Based on these, who could not come to a similar conclusion?"

At that moment, Wittmann stormed out of the prosecutor's office. He started running towards me in a frenzy, but by the time he got there, I slipped out of the ring of journalists, who, recognizing who was running between them, immediately threw themselves at him and didn't let him move.
What happened after this, I don't fully know, but I was sure that I took control of my case.

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Seven
paragraphs: Weeks went by. Initially, I found it hard to cope with Wright's removal. Every fiber of my being recoiled at the thought of speaking even a single word to Murphy Wittmann, who couldn't do anything to me because of all the public attention. He was forced to accept the fact that I would do things my own way, and although he looked at me with hatred every time, he still insisted that I report to him periodically. At times like this, just as dogs sense when they are facing a bad person, red flags would start flying inside me. Every time he called me into his office, I felt as though I wasn't really answering him, but was passing information directly to Mortenstein. It was as if Voldemort were living in his head, and he spoke with Mortenstein's voice.

But I didn't lose any sleep over it. Thanks to my new strategy, I seemed to be able to turn my luck around. I was invited to speak on shows, and after a few sessions I was able to enjoy the situation. Many people recognized me on the street. It was strange.

When I was young, like so many girls, I dreamed of becoming an actress, a dancer, or both. Thanks to Disney, so many had walked that path, so why couldn't it happen to me? Of course, the chances of a ten-year-old dreaming in a children's home were practically zero. Yet now, the whole country knew who I was, and somewhere deep down, that little girl felt happy about it.

But my other half, the adult Amanda, knew all too well that every wonder only lasts three days, and those who adore me today might be dragging my name through the mud tomorrow. I didn't buy into people's sweet talk, and I steered clear of the comment sections under my videos.

There was one thing I couldn't block out, though. Ads kept popping up on YouTube and TV at the most random times, portraying me as a vile liar and a cheap whore. I didn't know how to handle it. At first, it crushed me, and I felt they were succeeding in intimidating me, but each time I concluded that no matter how hard they tried, truth was on my side. After a while, I actually wanted to know what kind of garbage they were making up about me. I even felt a sense of pride that they had to resort to such tactics against me.

The trial was scheduled for July 21. Until then, there was still a month and a half, and I vowed that when this was all over, no matter what the verdict was, I would travel with Anton to some tropical island for several months and completely shut out the rest of the world. For some reason, I was extremely attracted to this idea. Knowing nothing, just enjoying one of the paradises on earth.

But I still had one major problem. I wanted to punish Jessica's killer. And although I knew for a fact that Jake did it, he had refused to speak to me ever since I lured him out in the Liberty district using Mike's picture. I had no idea where he had gone. Physically I did, of course, but who knows where Jake 'wandered' or what he did without Jeff having the slightest clue.
So the Jake case didn't go well. There was nothing I could concretely link to Jess's murder, even though I had known it since the moment the car was found with the handbrake on.
In addition, the investigation progressed promisingly. I was sure that we would manage to catch the president, but we still had to find answers to a few things.

For instance, it wasn't clear at all why it had to be Jake who killed Jessica, and we couldn't find out who gave Wilson his orders. The hitman's number was in his phone, but we couldn't link it to the president. Unresolved past cases, like the deaths of Mike Alioglu or Katherine, certainly hinted at this connection, but they didn't sufficiently prove that Wilson was anything more to the Neon Nights than a easily bribable, corrupt detective.

The girls who succeeded at Neon Nights also posed a puzzle. Their testimonies were well-documented and backed up by several others. There was no way to poke holes in them. We had to accept that the Neon Nights Jess described and the Neon Nights experienced by the likes of Lisa Bennet had absolutely nothing in common. That didn't mean they were mutually exclusive, of course. Rather, it highlighted the president's total lack of social empathy. Yet, we still hadn't found the link between the two places, even though it felt like something incredibly simple and obvious that we were just overlooking.

I discussed the problematic details with Anton at home countless times, but we didn't get anywhere. We always got stuck somewhere. Obviously, he couldn't investigate Wilson. Wilbur and his team were trying to unravel that lead with the help of Officer McRae, and I didn't expect Anton to do that anyway. I just wanted him to spot some detail that I was too close to see.

We were talking about this today as well, and no matter how hard we tried, we couldn't think of anything new. I wanted to go to the prosecutor's office in the afternoon, but now I was still trying to drag out the morning routine as long as possible, so I had been in the kitchen for about half an hour to meticulously prepare breakfast, a simple fried egg.
Anton was sitting at the table, reading the news while slurping his coffee. It annoyed me.
"Please don't do that," I told him.
"I was just drinking," he replied.
"You don't drink, you slurp. You can drink without making that noise."
"Sorry," he said, and walked out into the living room.
I didn't want him to go out, but I didn't know what to do.
"Don't certain sounds bother you?" I asked aloud, not wanting it to be my fault that he had to go out. He didn't answer, so I went to the living room. "Are you not bothered by sounds?"
"Actually, yes."
"Like what?"
"A few words," he answered. "But they're annoying words."
"Such as?" I asked him.
"Like 'kiddo'. It drives me absolutely crazy."
"I get it, so if I started saying kiddo this, kiddo that, like, oh, the little kiddo did this and that, the kiddos played kiddo games with the kiddo, and the kiddo-sitter..."
"Okay, okay, stop it! Yes, obviously it's annoying. But I don't make that slurping sound on purpose. I get that it bothers you, I'll watch out."

"How stupid the brain is sometimes," I mused. "Why do certain noises or words irritate us? Some people actually like those words, while others claw at the walls. There are quite a few like that—like the word 'thumb'. In Hungarian, it's literally 'inch-finger'. What does that even mean? That they measured something with it that was an inch? Or did the inch get its name because of the finger? But then what did it originally mean? It makes no sense."
"Or the tummy-dweller, and the bro."
"Do you hate 'bro'?"
"Is that a question? How irritating, Amy. When a stranger walks up to you and says, bro! I am definitely not his bro."

"What really annoys me is when people get grammar wrong. I want to rip the face off anyone who says 'should of' or 'smaller then me'. It's 'than'! 'Than'! 'Then' means something completely different."
"You're right. And then there are those stupid little songs or tunes that crawl into your ear, and when you're at your lowest and feeling your worst, they start echoing in your brain."
"Like Baby Shark."
"And the Chicken Song."
"The Pen Pineapple Apple Pen..."

"Or that old song about the cuckoo. I can't recall a single word from it except 'cuckoo' at the end of every line. And when you brought up what Jess's lawyer messaged last time, that tune was stuck in my head for days. I'm sure it'll stay there for another two days now that I've remembered it again."
"You're a genius, Anton!" I cried out. "You're a genius! The cuckoo! That's the damn word we've been looking for!"
"Who was looking for it?"
"We were! Jessica didn't send that message through Bill for nothing. It's not just you who can't stand it, Anton—Jake can't either! That's the key to it, I'd bet my life on it."
"And what do you want to do now?"
"Interrogate him."
"Don't you want to test it first?"
"I know I'm right. There's no other way this message makes any sense. I'll lay the groundwork, and then we'll question Jake in a way he won't easily forget."
"Maybe you shouldn't go there alone."
"I won't be alone, and I won't be the one questioning him either. There are much better people for that on the force."
"And if he says nothing?"
"Confronting him again with the fact that we know exactly what he did will be more than enough. One way or another, we're going to corner him."
