chapters.title: Chapter Twenty-Eight
paragraphs: A detective named Derek and I went to the sanatorium alone. He was a lot trickier than you'd think at first glance. He was a short, skinny man, his hair was frayed here and there in the worst places, and his appearance almost made people dislike him. However, his voice exuded a calmness as if he were a therapist. This quality made him a really pleasant companion, which was reinforced by his unmistakable perfume scent.

Jeff was not alone. In addition to his lawyer, a nurse and a doctor were also in the room. The latter considered it absolutely important to point out that Jefferson had not been in contact with the outside world since he was brought in, so he emphatically asked us not to bother him with things that have since become public. Of course, I had a hard time believing this. I was sure he found a way to talk to the president. True, he could have done this even before he was brought here.
We were seated around a larger table, even though we didn't come to negotiate, we just wanted to learn the truth from someone who had been living a lie for some time.
"What's your name?" Derek asked as a warm-up.
"Jefferson Morriset," Jeff replied.
"What do you do for a living?"
"I am an accountant."
"What was your relationship with Jessica Marsh?"
"We lived together."
"How long?"
"Until February 12, 2022. Until Jess died."
"And what was the cause of death?"
"A car accident, actually," replied Jefferson, summarizing the well-known story.
"Can you explain how it happened?"
"We left Montaukville for an evening performance, but on the way we hit a tunnel entrance."
"Why?"
"Because a foreign car, a Ford Mustang GT, pushed us off the road."
"What did that car look like?"
"It was black."
"Had you never seen it before?"
"No."
"Had you seen one like that before?" Derek asked.
"A few times. But only the way everyone else has."
"Didn't its sound seem familiar?"
"No," Jeff replied. "Why would it be? I cannot recognize a Mustang just by its sound. I like cars, but I'm not that obsessed."
"Do you remember how the accident happened?"
"We were being followed, but I don't remember the actual impact."
"Was Jessica afraid?"
"No. I remember I was the one who told her that I thought we were being followed. She didn't care. She said I was imagining things."
"But it's pretty obvious when you're being followed, isn't it?"

"I don't know. I found it odd, but I can't tell you exactly when it started to seem suspicious to me. There's only one road from Montaukville to Riverdale. Anyone heading there has to tail the cars in front of them for a long time, because there are few straight stretches and it's impossible to overtake."
"Do you remember being run off the road?"
"Not completely."
"Then isn't it possible that it was just an accident?"
"I don't know," Jeff replied.
"Why are you uncertain about this?" Derek asked back.

"Because Jessica had been threatened before she withdrew her charges against the president. I was so worried about her before, I thought she might be in danger. But after that, what reason would they have had to hurt her?"
"We don't know, that's what we want to find out," replied the detective. "How long were you followed by the Mustang?"
"Almost from the very start."
"And was there a stretch before that where they could have overtaken you?"
"At first, yes," Jeff replied, "but I didn't think they wanted to pass us. I was driving pretty fast myself."
"Did you see how many people were in the car?"
"No. It was pitch black. At that time of night, on a public road, it's impossible to tell who is inside the car."
"And you didn't know them?"
"No!" Jeff replied, growing more nervous. "How could I have known them if I couldn't even see who was sitting in the car?"
"That makes perfect sense," Derek stated. "Indeed, when it's dark, it's impossible to determine how many people are in a car. Yet you speak of them in the plural every time. Why?"
Jeff fell silent. He had no idea why he was speaking in the plural. I could see him trying to think the matter through.
"You don't have to answer these questions, Jefferson," the lawyer interjected.
"Yes, I know," Jeff acknowledged, "but I want to." With that, he turned to Derek. "I don't know why," he finally said. "For some reason, I always thought there was more than one of them."
"I see," the detective noted. "Do you happen to remember who called the ambulance?"
"No."
"A married couple who came from the opposite direction."
"I didn't know that. I had no memory of them."
"Do you know what the rest of the road from the tunnel to Riverdale is like?"
"It's winding all the way. No villages or other towns along it."
"And what about intersections?"
"There aren't many of those either."

"Yes, there really aren't. In fact, there are so few that the oncoming car had already passed the last intersection towards Riverdale before they reached the tunnel, and they didn't see anyone coming the other way."
"That's not so surprising," Jeff replied. "The ones who were following us could have turned around right after the crash."

"True. But a few minutes after the emergency services were notified, another car arrived at the scene of the crash from Montaukville, and they didn't see any oncoming vehicles either. How is that possible?"

"What are you trying to say?" Jefferson demanded, puzzled. "I know what I saw. I know there was a car there. Just because I'm in a sanatorium, don't treat me like a fool!" he snapped. He was struggling with being cornered.
"I don't think you're a fool, take it easy, Jefferson. I'm just stating the facts. That car could have disappeared from view in countless other ways, say on a side road in the forest."
"Jefferson, please listen to me and don't answer the detective's questions," the lawyer interjected again. "I want to end this right now."
"We won't," I interrupted. "We are treating Jefferson as a suspect, and right now, we are working to let him clear his name."
"Really?" the lawyer countered. "You have a very interesting way of working."
"Sir," Derek continued, "we still have a few questions to ask, but in truth, Jefferson is not the main person we are looking to for answers."
"If you want to talk to Jake Cooper, I'm afraid you are going to run into a brick wall. It's been several weeks since he last made contact with us. He is a complete law unto himself."

I was well aware of that, of course, but I hadn't come here for information. Jefferson fidgeted nervously in his chair, and I could tell he was still hiding something from us that he preferred not to talk about.
"Is there anything you want to talk about, Jefferson?" I asked.
"No," he replied, quick and brief.
"Then perhaps let's switch conversation partners," I suggested, and smugly, completely sure of myself, I leaned back in my chair.
"What are you planning to do?" asked Jeff's lawyer.
"Miss Evans has a theory on how to lure Jake Cooper out," the detective replied.
"That's fantastic news!" the lawyer said sarcastically. "And what exactly does it take?"
"Nothing special," I replied. "Just a trigger word. Like... cuckoo."
Jefferson's face suddenly changed.
"Are you thinking that, like in some dumb spy movie, you can use a trigger word to activate Jefferson's alter ego?"
"Yes, exactly," I replied. "And I mean specifically this word: cuckoo."
"Don't you dare say that word again!" Jeff cut in.
"And why not?" I asked. "Because Jake Cooper can't stand the word cuckoo?"
At that moment, it wasn't just the expression on Jeff's face that transformed, but his entire gaze.
"Go to hell, Alice Bucks!" Jake spat out. "Go to hell, you stinking bitch!"
"How dare you speak to the prosecutor like that?!" Detective Derek snapped. "Don't try to provoke the prosecution with rumors!"

"Jake, please don't say anything!" the lawyer interjected. "And don't insult the prosecutor either! For now, this will be overlooked, given how underhanded the investigators' tactic was, but don't cross the line!"
"Now, now," I said, trying to defuse the tension. "I'm really not easily offended, and certainly not petty enough to take a suspect's personal attacks to heart in a situation like this."
Jake seemed a bit lost. He didn't understand why everyone had suddenly intervened.

"I'm not saying anything," he stated flatly. "You can leave now. But this woman is indeed Alice Bucks, Jessica's close friend, so she has no right to be here. She's involved in this. You'll see for yourselves. Did you come for the truth? Well, you got it."
It was the first time I saw the lawyer look uneasy, almost angry. On Derek's lips, however, a faint but noticeable smile appeared.

"It's fine," I cut in before anyone could divert attention from the main point. "We understand. According to you, I'm Alice Bucks and I was Jessica's friend. But would you tell me who you heard that from?"
"Nobody. I haven't spoken to anyone since I was brought here."
"Not even with your lawyer?" I inquired.
"Jake, don't answer!" the lawyer spoke again in a commanding voice, but Jake still didn't pay attention to him.
"No one. What difference does it make?" he shot back, huffy. He didn't even notice that he had already given us what we came for.

"Then how do you know Alice Bucks?" Derek asked. "Jake could only know her from the Neon Nights! Did this rumor about the prosecutor originate with you?" The lawyer tried to end the interrogation, exasperated.

"Thank you very much for bringing that up," I said to Jake calmly. "You see, we didn't even have to cross-examine you to get you to admit that you were part of the Neon Nights, and that you're associated with Edgar Mortenstein."
colors: gray
warm white

It worked! I thought to myself. I finally managed to extract some sort of confession out of Jake. I was satisfied with the interrogation; Derek had done a good job. A trial, no matter how precisely one prepares for it, doesn't always go exactly as planned. Both sides try to keep their main trump cards hidden from each other until the moment they have to land the first blows, and if we're lucky, nothing comes up that we hadn't accounted for.

Although we willingly answered the questions of the press, we could not give them everything. This was partly due to legal obstacles and partly strategic. Because of the publicity, it may have seemed to many that we were conducting a completely transparent investigation, which, of course, was also a tactic to keep our opponents off-balance.

It was clearly working. Mortenstein and his circle were getting nervous. They hadn't expected us to strike back. Damaging articles began to appear about the relationship between Wittmann and Mortenstein; it had never been a secret, but now it seemed far more intriguing than before. The president gave clumsy answers to questions probing the matter. The Chief Prosecutor obviously owed his position to political decisions rather than professional merit.

In addition, there was the Jake thread too, which in itself couldn't yet overthrow Mortenstein's power—since anyone can be an acquaintance of a suspected killer—but the knowledge that Jake might still be working for him fired everyone up.

At noon that day, I was waiting in our usual restaurant for Anton, who was being held up by his editor, when suddenly five men in black suits appeared and sat down in various parts of the dining area. I found the scene strange right up until Edgar Mortenstein stood before me in the flesh and, without asking, took the seat reserved for Anton. That's what you get when you're late, I thought, annoyed. A president immediately steals your spot.

I was shaking. I didn't even have time to react to it, it came so unexpectedly, it completely upset me. I felt like my face was turning into a winter landscape, while drops of water from a hot storm dripped down my forehead. I've never seen this man like that before. His narrow eyes and thin mouth gave off an austerity, his scent was masculine yet fresh, and his jacket lapel was decorated with a jeweled pin. A well-known yet unknown figure sat in front of me.
"Taken," I snapped at him immediately, I didn't even know how, because I hadn't felt so uncomfortable in a long time.
The president reacted to my attempt with silent laughter.
"Good day, Miss Evans," he said.
"My, you know my name?" I asked with irony in my voice, still chalking up my outspoken style to embarrassment rather than courage.
"In politics, you know, the rules are quite flexible. Sometimes you can do something, sometimes you can't. I'm an experimental type."
"I hope you know that what you are doing now is completely illegal."
"And you know that you won't raise an objection because of it."
"Why wouldn't I?"

"Because you like a clean game, don't you?" he inquired, but the sentence carried too many implications for me to be sure I understood it correctly. "I just wanted to meet you in person," he reassured me. "Please don't take it as an intrusion..." and then he finished the sentence while looking into my eyes: "Miss Evans, Madam Prosecutor."
"Why are you repeating my name?" I asked.
"They say we have met already, but I think I would remember if that had been so."
"It would probably have stayed with me too if that had been so," I repeated.
"I owe you an apology. The media has obviously crossed all boundaries. I didn't consider what I might cause you. I'm sorry."
I felt literally nauseous. It might seem strange, but I was glad. Finally, I felt something simple and clear.
"It's too early for you to apologize," I answered. "Besides, there's no need. No one who puts his hand to the plow should look back."
"You are versed in classical education; I like that," Mortenstein noted.
"I would like to point out that it is becoming increasingly difficult for me not to view this meeting as unlawful tampering."

"Then I really must go," he laughed. "I just felt I had to see you," he explained defensively. "Believe it or not, we are on the same side. We both want the truth to prevail. I trust you, Amanda!" and he drove his point home by gently taking my hand.
He stood up and walked away. Just as quickly as he had come, he vanished. I hadn't even recovered from my shock by the time Anton arrived.
"Mortenstein was just here," I began.
"The president?" he asked, surprised.
"No, the actor... why are you asking stupid questions?"
"Did he threaten you?"

"Why would he threaten me? I mean... yeah, surely... but I didn't even grasp how he did it. He just showed up and sat in your seat. Why the hell do you have to be late right when this man shows up? I don't know what he did, but I'm still shaking."
"Did he say anything?" He too seemed rattled by this unexpected visit.
"Of course he did. He said he was sorry, and called me 'Miss Evans', and said he didn't know me."
"I don't fully understand."

"I don't get it either," I replied at a loss. "He came into the restaurant with five guys in suits, and then sat down. I told him it was taken. He said, 'Miss Evans,' to which I said, 'Oh, so you know my name?' To that, he said that in politics all means are flexible. I said it's illegal to try to influence the prosecutor before the trial, and he said that was obvious, but he wanted to see me because apparently he doesn't even know me. You don't say! At that, he made excuses: sorry, he went too far. And I was like, alright, this is already tampering with the prosecution, and then he left just as he came. That's how it happened, except almost none of the words were actually said like that."
"What the hell was this?" Anton asked the question that I too had been racking my brain on since Mortenstein left.
"Probably to make his presence felt, to make his power felt—that he can do it whenever he wants, just show up out of nowhere. These are very big beasts, Anton, these polar bears..."
"There is also a brown one among them..." he continued the well-known meme, then we fell silent.

It wasn't just that I had lost my appetite. I felt the situation was far more oppressive than that. A weight of several hundred pounds seemed to press down on every square centimeter of my body. That's how underwater pressure is usually described, though it's highly possible it's not just a metaphor; reality might be exactly like that, even if there is no one left to tell us how it feels, since the body would immediately crumble under such weight.

But the weight of what? What appeared that invisibly rushed at me with all its force? There was only one person here, barely one hundred and eighty centimeters tall, maybe not even that much, ninety kilos at the most. It doesn't seem that heavy. It was true that there was an aura of astonishment that I couldn't describe what it actually was, I just felt, with every square centimeter of my being, that it was already something, that it was already able to weigh on a person. But maybe it wasn't even justified by the fact that I had to resist him with all my strength. And that sound, yes, I can't take it lightly either, because even sitting in front of it is a very taxing, almost sweaty challenge, and the smell, the smell, the silence of shock, all of this is a weight that is placed on that body, attached as ballast and producing the heavy newtons, then the five hundred kilos of the suits, and the invisible pride of power, which I should be able to resist, and already I knew that's why he came, to show himself exactly, to let me know how damn hard it was all going to be, which as much as I wanted to imagine, I never knew.

I looked at Anton. Into Anton's sky-blue eyes, in which a tear glinted. He was afraid, or rather, afraid for me, yet his mouth smiled excitedly because he had sensed the gravity of the situation long before I did. And I had to realize that this tear wasn't just from concern—the idiot was unabashedly proud, because the country's most powerful man feared his lover like a little child who knows they've been caught, with no escape from punishment.

Mortenstein never gave a statement. He would have been a fool. Every unspoken statement was waiting for us to prove its truth ourselves. He was not so forthcoming as to respond in detail to the allegations. He fought against us with much more sophisticated means. The TV proclamations that he addressed to the country were not addressed to us, they were merely political tricks. He didn't afford the prosecution the courtesy of letting us ask him anything. He had every right to do so. As a defense attorney, I would have advised him to do the same, but regardless, I thought this strategy was petty and pathetic.

The president spoke when, where, and to whomever he pleased. I had accepted from the start that it would be this way, and it was better that way, because I never had to look him in the eye. For years, Mortenstein had been just a celebrity to me, occasionally appearing on certain channels, whom I tried to lock inside the plastic casing of the TV like some evil genie. It was easy just to think of him like that, easy to ignore him, easy to hide from him, but he realized that he could exert an influence on me simply by seeing me, by looking me in the eye. He felt he needed to meet me, because I was the one who held his fate in my hands, I was leading the investigation, and I alone could put him in prison. He needed to rattle me.
"You are terrible," I said. "Don't you see the situation? You should view what Mortenstein did as a threat, not be proud of me."
"It's hard for me to separate the two," Anton replied. "He's afraid of you. Why wouldn't I love that thought?"
"We already knew he was afraid of me. How is this any different?"
"That he went so far as to deliver the message in person. He packaged it as intimidation, but it won't work."
"And you like that?" I asked provocatively.
"That Mortenstein is afraid?" he smiled. "Love it!"
"I told you you're terrible," I said, caressing Anton's arm and leaving my hand there.
I could feel the goosebumps rise on his arm, and knew he was thinking of something ridiculously superficial. He smiled tellingly.
"If I didn't know you, I'd be worried." With that, I gestured toward the restroom. "Come on, then!" I ordered him.
Fortunately, there weren't many people, it was already lunchtime, and the place was empty. I took Anton's hand and led him to the toilet.
"By the way, everything was recently renovated," I noted. "We don't have to worry about hygiene, either."

Although the men's and women's sections had separate doors, we boldly entered with the sign "gentlemen" and pushed our way into one of the cabins, now kissing. It wasn't built up to the ceiling. Anyone could have heard anything.

We've always talked about it. After the bathroom cabin incident, I knew that it would happen one day, even if it is very difficult to foresee it, after all, when do people get into such a mood in a restaurant that they fall for each other right then and there? But now that Mortenstein had set up and stirred up the stagnant water, he had created a special occasion, and this was the one of many occasions when it finally happened.

Anton lifted my top in a few seconds and kissed my neck. I felt that we were attuned to each other very quickly. I unbuttoned his pants, then pushed them down below his knees, and finally he did the same with mine. We stood there facing each other with our pants down and I laughed to myself.
"Like some messed-up western," I remarked. "Who shoots first?"

He shot first. He grabbed my arms tightly and held them together above my head. He spun me around, pressed my hands against the wall, and bent me forward. When I got back, Anton was still reading his phone, but I immediately took it out of his hands.

chapters.title: Chapter Thirty
paragraphs: Anton was in the kitchen preparing French toast for breakfast when an angry and disappointed cry of frustration echoed from the bathroom.
"God damn it, fuck this shit!"
"What's wrong?" he asked, as if the exact same curse hadn't burst from my throat at unpredictable intervals.
"What do you think? When else would it happen if not now? My damn period started, today of all days. It just had to show up today."

We both fell silent. I heard Anton rummaging through the medicine cabinet and pulling out a painkiller, but my cramps hadn't even started yet; I was just fiddling with the tampon wrapper when he walked in.
"Are you out of your mind?" I snapped. "Don't you think this could have waited five minutes?"
"Right, I'm an idiot," he admitted, backing out of the bathroom with a pill and a glass of water in his hand.
Once I cleaned myself up, I felt like throwing a tantrum, but instead I decided to sneak up behind Anton and wrap my arms around his waist. He was standing at the stove, flipping the slices of bread.
"I'm upset that it started," I sighed. "I was hoping that once we started trying, it would happen right away."
"Think of all the pills and energy wasted," he teased. "If we'd known beforehand that having sex wouldn't result in a baby every single time, we could have taken things a bit easier."
"If only we could know which one would do it," I replied. "But I'm really enjoying the practice, so let's not stop..."
"I don't think you should worry about that," he answered and kissed the crown of my head.
Since the stunt at the restaurant, we had been having sex even more than before, and Anton had become so attentive that it was starting to get on my nerves.
"Let me help!" he'd say. "Don't lift anything heavy!"
"Anton!" I said. "Even if there were something in there, it would be about the size of a pea. What do you think is going to happen if I pick up a pot, a vacuum cleaner, or a washbasin?"
"I know, I know," he would reply.
"Then stop driving me crazy!"

But there were also times when I genuinely appreciated his pampering. He regularly came home with small gifts. Once he brought flowers, another time a Scrub Mommy, and another time, chocolates. The burning love in his eyes filled me with a wonderful warmth, which only strengthened my desire to have his baby. Anton hadn't changed, he was just paying closer attention to me—because that's just what happens when you and your partner decide to start a family.

What I liked most about him was how much he immersed himself in his role. I knew that no matter what, he would take care of us, and to the mom-to-be in me, that made him extremely manly. We talked many times before about what will happen to us when we have a family, what will happen to us if for some reason we don't have one. At the time, I wasn't sure what the future would bring, because I didn't dare to know. All my life, Anton was the only man I could trust, even though I could never accept the peace of certainty even with him, not even after he repeatedly risked his life for me. The future is distant and the threads from which it was woven are so inextricable, I always thought.
"And if it doesn't work out?" I brought up.
"Then we'll go to Disneyland by ourselves," he replied. "With you, I'll always have a princess I can take there."
"You're sappy, but it's sweet," I let it slide.

Anton always played down unpleasant thoughts. It didn't fit in his life to deal with inconveniences, although I would have liked him to say something more soothing. Of course, it could easily be that he didn't mean it as a joke, but this solution was so far from the real problems that I couldn't take it seriously. But for now, I had to let it go. I simply didn't have time to deal with my fears about starting a family; the trial of the Mortenstein case was starting, and I had to go through so many documents that a week wouldn't have been enough.
"Where is Hermione's testimony?" Anton asked.
After a short search, I showed him the bundle of witness testimonies.
"Where is the expert report on Jeff's BMW?"
I immediately pointed to another stack.
"And where are the materials on Jake?"
"To the right of the desk," I answered.
"Then what's the issue?" he asked. "You know everything inside out, so why are you so nervous?"
I hated it when someone tried to tell me whether I was allowed to be nervous. If I wanted to be nervous, I was; if I didn't, I wasn't. But neither state could be summoned on command.

"I don't know what you planned for today, Anton, but I will deal with these until 23:59, so whatever you feel like doing today or have felt like in recent years, go ahead! I swear to you, I don't even care if you go to a strip club."
"At half past eight in the morning?"
"Pardon me, Mr. Martin. Why don't you write to Google and ask them about their opening hours?"
"I picked you up there, honey, you danced there."
"Mhmm... Now scram!" With that, I had him out of the apartment within minutes.
(Anton Martin)

Amy has been working like crazy this past month. She brought home files by the pound, cluttering almost the entire living room with them. I was quite surprised, because over the last two weeks she had even skipped our usual weekly cleaning routine. I knew that required immense willpower on her part, but she had to accept that she wouldn't be able to read through everything thoroughly if she wasted her time tidying up. She finally gave up for good the last time she cleaned, when she put things away so well that it took her three days to find everything and return them to where she deemed logical. She decided not to experiment with cleaning anymore.
"Fine, fine! Then we'll just never clean again!" she grumbled to herself.

I headed toward the city center. It was brutally hot. I didn't want to drive; I felt that since I'd been kicked out of the house anyway, I might as well take public transit—it promised to be more interesting. My plan was to sit by the riverbank and watch people. I wanted to finish a book, for which I needed a few characters from the street, and the public squares were swarming with people like ants on hot summer asphalt back in my childhood. I bought a bottle of cola and a bag of peanuts at a convenience store. I could feel my brain slowly baking. Even though I retreated to a shaded bench, the air was as scorching as an oven. I couldn't focus on anything else.

I needed to get somewhere cool. I was afraid to ask myself the questions about global warming. I've gotten comfortable in recent years. I knew I had contributed to the problem, meaning I couldn't enjoy a damn day in the middle of July anymore, and I was angry with myself for it. Of course, also for politicians and public space planners, who want to solve every call for tenders with monstrous cobblestones and baby-sized trees. It wasn't good to sit there. I thought of the library, where I was sure that I would be able to spend some of my time pleasantly, the rest we will see.

Once inside, though, I couldn't resist the inviting aroma of the café. Entering the building felt like a breeze of salvation; my body cooled down instantly thanks to the pleasant 77-degree air being pumped through high-performance vents. I ordered a melange and a custard slice. It was the most cliché choice I could have made, but I wanted to play it safe. Having already been disappointed by both the park bench and the riverbank, I couldn't afford another blunder today. At the table next to mine, two elderly women were chatting. Lately, whenever we went out, I noticed that sooner or later people would start talking about the president and the investigation. Many recognized Amy, and occasionally me too, though fortunately the latter was rare. By now, I was almost instinctively listening to the chatter at nearby tables. Maybe I'd become a gossip, or maybe I just liked eavesdropping, I don't know. But today, these two ladies were telling each other about their grandchildren, and as they showed off their photos, an uneasiness spread through me. It was as if I were being called by another picture among the millions held captive in this library. Did it really take this? Did the boasting of two grandmothers unleash some secret that wanted to find me? Which picture wanted to reveal itself to me? Who did I want to see something about that I had never seen before?

I ran my fork through the custard slice. The fluffy cream split quietly in two. I had already devoured the top and bottom pastry layers, while the warm coffee slid smoothly down my throat. I played around with the plate. I put piece after piece of the cake into my mouth in tiny bites until finally only a crumbs remained. I downed the rest of my melange and headed toward the periodicals and daily newspapers. I could feel the trail getting warmer.

I didn't know what I was looking for, where to search, or for what period. Almost imperceptibly, the year 2008 came to mind. But what happened back then, I asked myself. The Olympics? But what would I want with the Beijing Olympics? The election?! Yes, that had to be it, though I would have preferred to forget it rather than remember. I relaxed. So that was it; that was what wanted to disrupt my peaceful coffee. But what exactly was I supposed to research? Just pull up a few daily papers and we'd be set? Like a man possessed, I caught myself whispering words aloud under my breath. I looked around, but no one paid me any attention—either they hadn't noticed, or they pretended not to. I went to a terminal and ordered issues from the first five daily newspapers that came to mind, dating from around the election. I'm an idiot. I knew it full well. I can't be sane. Silent ghosts are whispering in my brain, refusing to let me go until they get what they want.

I flipped through a Formula 1 magazine until the requested papers arrived. I have always had high respect for librarians, no matter which department they work in. I knew nothing about the logistics of how requests were retrieved. I had never been on a library tour, though I would have been fascinated. I imagined the old issues lined up in vast archives where entry was strictly restricted. I don't know why—perhaps so no one could mess up the order, ensuring some fool like me could never look into the past again. Then online newspapers crossed my mind. What if I had just typed the date into a search engine, and it immediately spat out the archived articles? No, no, I brushed the thought aside. I did the right thing by requesting the physical copies. Today, I wanted to trust the print media. What was set in print couldn't be erased, I deluded myself. Or was it simply the library's atmosphere that kept me from searching online?

With the newspapers in hand, I looked for a separate table where I could comfortably leaf through them in an armchair. First, I went through the Daily City. 'The election ended with the victory of Edgar Mortenstein! The previous government lies in ruins...' the newspaper wrote, without any exaggeration. The previous administration had failed miserably, and back then, even in me, the flames of hope still flickered. I was amazed at how much younger Mortenstein looked. It was as if it weren't even him, just someone who looked exactly like him, but that is the essence of photographs. They capture a moment in time that will never return. There was also a group photo. They were celebrating the victory, some standing alone, others with their families on the podium before a shapeless crowd. I pulled out another paper. Love City News: 'Mortenstein went big yesterday, sweeping two-thirds of the constituencies!' That got me thinking. We owed a lot to that outcome. The photo showed the stage from a similar angle, but with a slightly different framing of the people. Mortenstein was preparing to give his speech. Then the third, the fourth, and finally the last newspaper showed the moment in nearly the same way. Nobody wanted to be different; they all wanted to illustrate the grand success with celebratory pictures. A heavy excitement ran through me. I didn't know yet what I had missed, but I knew that what was calling to me from within was right in front of my eyes. I placed the photos side by side. Everything about them looked nearly identical. I tried to identify the people on stage. The third row was barely visible, the second only slightly better. But in the front row, everyone was clear. Mortenstein, the woman who was currently deputizing for him—whose name always seemed to prompt some event whenever it was mentioned—the finance minister, the interior minister guy, party officials, and a few children. Among them, in the front row, was a curly-haired boy of about twelve. Then he appeared in the second row. Finally, he was visible at the side, just leaving the stage. There were other family members too. The vice president, for instance, held his little daughter in his arms, while the interior minister guy held the hand of one of his teenage sons. The communications director smiled between his two daughters, and all three were applauding. You could almost see how, in the next moment, he would raise their arms like actors taking a bow. But where did the other child go? Why did he leave, and how did he get there in the first place? Whose child was he? Did he have no one to share his joy with? Was there no one to hold his hand? Who was this boy, calling out to me from the news pages while I was eating my custard slice? I pulled out my phone and searched for archived articles. I found earlier moments of the same scene. In those, Mortenstein wasn't yet standing at the pulpit; he was further back, with a curly-haired boy by his side.

chapters.title: Chapter Thirty-One
paragraphs: Who could that boy be? I asked myself this morning while lying in bed. Amy was already getting ready, she got up at six, even though the trial didn't start until noon. He obviously still had a lot to do. I didn't dare say anything to him. I didn't want to mess it up. His focus was completely elsewhere, and this nothingness would only have served to distract him from his precisely planned agenda.
"How old was Jess?" I asked Amy.
"Doesn't it matter?"
"It doesn't matter" I answered.
"It was 27" he answered briefly. "He was born in 95. What is this for you?"
"I just wanted to know how many years older you were."
"You already knew, but with two" Amy replied. "It really doesn't seem like much, does it?"
"The two years or the 27?"
"None of them."
"Because none of them are many" I established.
"Jessica Marsh lived 27 years" he said, as the minister had said at his funeral, and then he was silent.
"Sorry, I didn't mean to disturb you" I spoke again. "Get ready, I was just asking."
"I don't think it would be a problem if you reminded me how little Jess lived. Damn little. He lived a very short life. It shouldn't have taken that much..."

The courtroom is full of people. I dressed elegantly, I wanted anyone who recognized me to see that Amy was getting all the support I could. He wore a dark blue suit. With perfect elegance, with matching high heels. Her blonde hair fell like gold on her shoulders, she even went to the nail salon at 8 in the morning. He stuck a small judge's gavel on his ring finger, as if he was betrothed to justice. He choreographed everything he could think of. I really liked this care, it represented well how he prepared for this trial. I was proud of him.

Mortenstein wasn't in the room yet, but I knew he might arrive at any moment. I was waiting for the press staff to get excited when he arrived. Amy stood up and read the indictment she had written months earlier. I knew he knew it from the outside. He said it 99X without paper, and in the end he didn't make a single mistake in it. There was no need for this, yet he wanted it that way. I thought I discovered Athena Wright in the gallery. He liked Amy and I knew how much he wanted the president behind bars because of her.

The journalists started clicking wildly with their cameras. The president appeared in the hall like a celebrated celebrity, with bodyguards following him, a true police escort. Although Mortenstein was a defendant, there was no outward indication that he was under arrest. It wasn't. He defended himself on the loose, he only had to keep certain limits. Anno showed up at the restaurant illegally, but the attorney general did everything he could to make Mortenstein feel as comfortable as possible amid the charges. That said, there was no danger involved. If he had run away, he would have confessed his guilt, anyway, he was too big a man to be able to hide. Whatever he believed about the truth, he thought he would swim, and I was repulsed by this arrogance.

Amy looked behind her in confusion. During Mortenstein's entrance, he was looking at him the whole time, he wanted to make him uncertain, but I knew that all his efforts were unnecessary. Amy was long past doubting herself. The discrediting in the media only made it stronger.

Along with Mortenstein, Jake also arrived, although he was followed by nurses instead of bodyguards. Too comfortable for him, I thought. He will swim. It was hard for me to see him as Jeff, even if Jess and Amy probably wanted him that way.
Their lawyers were like two peas in a pod.
After a few minutes, the judge finally appeared and the room rose to welcome him.
"Dear Court!" spoke up...
And with this it began...

The judge must have been around sixty years old. Amy had told me about him before, but I hadn't memorized his name, and of course I'd never seen him before. He was considered a professional authority among judges, taught at university, wrote many books, and did not seem like someone who could be influenced by power. I looked at this as if Amy was born under a lucky constellation after all. There was nothing unusual about that. That's how things should work. The independence of the court is fundamental, and only conspirators should have concerns about it. Of course, there are exceptions everywhere, and in the last decade it was easy to believe that Mortenstein had succeeded in dismantling the system of checks and balances, but the reality seemed different, and I honestly wanted to believe that.

Now it was Amy who made the accusation. The water broke, I was overwhelmed with heat, I was sweating under my jacket. It was cool in the room, but I would have felt the same way in a Finnish ice bath. He said things like: forced labor, human trafficking, child prostitution, and I thought how could this even happen? How could these things happen to people in a country that outwardly radiates the appearance of perfection, a country where perfection has become an export, and I was disgusted by it. What kind of world is it where this is happening right in front of our eyes, yet we don't know about it, or even worse, we don't even want to be aware of it.

I remembered how Amy and I met. My editor said he would introduce me to the director, because he is a big and serious man and has a lot of experience in publishing books. In any case, they wanted to publish my novel, which at first I thought was the level I could take on in front of the public. They thought it would be an exciting, good crime story, and it was, and in their great happiness that I had chosen them, they said that the business should be celebrated in a place that was worthy of the career I was about to pursue. Everything that wasn't taught in high school, is nevertheless essential for those who wanted to find a job in one of the similar fields. Everyone loved the dance lessons, but we also learned the drier etiquette with pleasure, because they wanted to make real gentlemen out of us, and we wanted to become one too."
"We understand" Amy summarized what Lisa had to say, then continued. "How long have you been attending Neon Nights classes since then?"
"For four years. I don't know exactly, it should be calculated. Maybe from 2013 to 17."
"He has said this before, so presumably the interval is correct" Amy reassured him. "How would you describe the girls at Neon Nights?"
"I don't want to offend anyone" began Lisa Bennet, "but whoever got in there was most likely a real A-category young girl."
"What does category A young girl mean?"

"Girls who had the right background to take advantage of Neon Nights, and I don't just mean financially. A neon nightsos was definitely dedicated enough to make the most of every moment, and his upbringing was impeccable, so to speak. Many of us attended private schools, we received the best education, everything was given to us to succeed."
"What do you mean by success?" Amy inquired further.

"Several became actors, singers, dancers, and well-known models. But I am sure that even those who did not step into the limelight still benefit from what they learned there. You can tell from afar if you've been to Neon Nights."
"Were there girls who grew up in, say, worse conditions?"

"We didn't know where everyone was from. My girlfriends mostly came from better-off families. Obviously we all knew each other. There weren't enough of us to walk past each other on the street as strangers, but I didn't know how everyone got there. I heard there was a scholarship program for those whose families weren't wealthy, but it wasn't clear which girl was receiving the grant. Everyone was treated the same."
"Did someone not complete the training?"

"Oh, how!" snapped Lisa. "Of course. Not everyone could handle the pace dictated by the course leaders. I remember more than once we walked five kilometers in ten-centimeter high heels. Can you imagine how that felt? By the end, everyone's feet were covered in blood. Obviously, this was not always the case. Anyway, it turned out to be a useful experience, they pushed our limits."
"Did a lot of people complain about things being taken so strictly in Neon Nights?"
"We were schoolgirls, many people complained, but now everyone realizes how much we owed to this method."
"And what happened to those girls who left the training?"
"I understand they had to pay back the scholarship."
"And if they weren't on scholarship?"

"Some of them too. I don't know exactly, but there was a commitment from the department of families. The parents of the girls who came from wealthy families must have contracted differently than those who could not afford the training at all."
"How should this be understood?" Amy asked. "He seemed to smell blood."

"I don't know exactly. I did not write these contracts, nor do I know which girl was there with such support. But the news spread that they had signed a ten thousand dollar scholarship with them for one year."
"Not many people left the training then, I think" Amy acknowledged.

"Not a few. You would think that ten thousand dollars is still a visible amount, wouldn't you think. For someone whose family is not rich, it can be a real challenge to extract it, of course it had to be seen as an investment. Despite this, quite a few left Neon Nights during the year, regardless of whether they were on scholarship or not."
"Why did Neon Nights offer scholarships to less fashionable girls?"

"From investment. It's a deal, I guess. Presumably, it would have been repaid from later works. There were quite a few talents among them. I support this attitude, and I think it was a very nice idea on the part of the Edgars. Uncle Eddie is sensitive to social issues, probably because he's a politician."

I suddenly burst out laughing loudly, which I immediately bit back, of course I thought I could detect signs of disgust on Amy's face. Edgar Mortenstein and social sensitivity was a veritable oxymoron to everyone, yet this girl talked about it as if she were at least testifying for Martin Luther King.
"How did the participants recoup this investment after they left the training?" Amy asked Lisa.

"I don't even know how the scholarship was awarded exactly" she objected. "Why are you asking me such a thing? I have no idea about it" looked at the president. "Uncle Eddie can certainly help you with this matter."
"I think so too" Amy replied calmly. "but the President has refused to testify, and I cannot compel him to speak of it."
"I understand" Lisa replied. "Well then there is nothing to do, you have to find someone else who knows this" he acknowledged enthusiastically.
"Do you think it is conceivable that there were girls who worked this repayment in, say, another place?" Amy tried to steer the conversation towards the other Neon Nights.
"What are you thinking?"
"Say, as sex workers."
"Jesus!" Lisa Bennet sighed. "How do you come up with such a thing? We studied in a professional system, don't make me laugh with such theories."
"I think I raised a realistic possibility. Why are you so aloof from him?"
"I don't even respond to that" she scorned. "I find this unimaginable."
"Why do you consider it so?" Amanda went on prying.
"I have 100% trust in those who provided us with these opportunities. That's all I can add to that."

Lisa Bennet was genuinely outraged by Amy's idea, even though it was a perfectly realistic suggestion that insolvent girls were being used as sex workers. Although at first we all protested against accepting that an inverse Neon Nights had to exist, in the end we had to realize that it was nothing more than a devilishly designed trap, which was no less than an investment. In fact, it was the only real one. Those who were successful and rich could, thanks to their background, pump huge amounts of money into Neon Nights training, and they did so with pleasure. They thought they were exclusive, and in the form they experienced, the place really gave them what it promised. Well-to-do families presumably easily paid off the debt for their back-dancing daughters, and were perhaps more ashamed that they didn't make it to the end than outraged by the harshness of the training. The girls from less fortunate backgrounds, but persistent and talented, could pay off their debts from their later jobs, while those who stepped back from them could find themselves in the Neon Nights of Mordor. The idea was brilliant. And Amy had to connect the two places somehow.
"Lisa, I have one more question for you" Amy said. "Have you ever experienced any signs of sexual abuse at Neon Nights?"

"I haven't experienced anything like that. We had professional teachers, most of them women. They were tough, but they didn't touch anyone with a new one. By the way, special emphasis was also placed on sexual education. Sessions were held by sexologists and intimacy coordinators. Believe me, I'm telling the truth when I say Neon Nights was decent in every way."
"Thanks!" Amy replied and sat down at her desk.

Now it was the lawyer's turn. I haven't quite figured out their strategy yet. Thinking with the head of a crime writer, I tried to see the most unexpected things in the background, but Mortenstein's side, as if he didn't want to deny anything, rather tried to make the Neon Nights phenomenon look like a series of misunderstandings. It was clear that they also accepted it, there was a place where girls were sexually exploited, but they skillfully covered up that they had anything to do with it. One could almost feel that they too had become victims of some sophisticated abuse.
"How are you?" the lawyer asked with attentiveness in his voice, but Lisa seemed caught unexpectedly by this kindness.
"Thank you, quite well" he answered curtly, narrowing his eyes.
"Please describe what the Neon Nights where you held your trainings looked like."

"Like a palace" she exaggerated. "It was a beautiful building in the city center. Three floors, snow-white walls, marble columns. Neon Nights itself was not intrusive. I mentioned earlier during the hearing that we were obliged to maintain confidentiality when signing the contract, and this approach was also reflected in his placement. Only on the intercom was a barely noticeable inscription. It wasn't advertised anywhere. Incidentally, Hermés was also in the same building on Avenue Brillante, with Cartier next to it. It was really motivating to enter the building even as a teenager. But now I don't know what's been working there since it stopped, which I'm really sorry for anyway..."

Lisa chattered. Although he did not answer what the lawyer asked, he seemed to want to cut it. This made me believe him even more sincerely when he talked about how special he felt in the environment that his rich family and circle of friends created for him. She was treated like a real gentleman, and I knew then that Lisa Bennet's testimony was going to be a dead end for Amy. He was obviously telling the truth. Its impeccable manners and appearance showed from afar that it was the result of the careful work of professionals. I envied him because of Amy. I knew for a fact that Neon Nights of You was Amy's dream, but instead she was banished to the Brimstone Hell. I was angry at the world. Then I looked at Amanda and I was filled with infinite pride. I remembered how Mortenstein had treated her in the bistro. He was afraid of her. Amy's life journey was a middle finger up to this world, and I couldn't look at it without admiration.

"The interior was created based on carefully compiled plans. In its mood, it matched the style outside. It was furnished with quality furniture and was definitely not over the top or intrusive. I loved going there."
"And was there any reference to the Neon Nights inside the building?" the lawyer asked.

"Neon Nights operated on the entire third floor, which was taken up by a private elevator, and of course there was a sign that it was there. At the entrance, a sign indicated what was on the other side of the door, while in the lobby, there was a neon, yet discreet sign."
"What did this inscription look like?"
"I'd rather call it a logo. In a pink circle, white and blue NN slipped into each other. Neon Nights was signed in small letters in a semicircle. I can still see it before my eyes."
"And what did the name Neon Nights mean? What did it want to refer to?" the lawyer went on inquiring.

"It may seem corny to today's eyes, but in the mid-2010s there was a renaissance of neon lights and it hinted at what we wanted to achieve. We wanted to be the light at the galas, at the big events of social life."

The lawyer, it seemed, did not want to keep Lisa up for long. He asked him a few more things, for example, what kind of person he knew Mortenstein to be, and he said that the president was one of the best people in the world, which, let's face it, could not be considered an unbiased statement on his part, but nobody expected him to say anything other than what he thought. Lisa Bennet was honest. After the girl's appearance, the police carefully looked into who she really was, and in every detail the reality matched what she said. She was an international model who was active mainly in Europe, and more recently in the Far East, as an ambassador for countless long-established brands. He was a celebrated celebrity in his profession, and most importantly, he was as pure as snow. He really owed everything to Neon Nights, and it was impossible to expect him to say even one bad word, or even the president who made it possible for him. If they wanted credibility for Neon Nights, they got it. They could hardly have found a better person for this purpose than Lisa Bennet. She shone in the Neon Nights sky as promised upon her entry. He said something else, then left the room, and I felt uneasy. Not because of Lisa. His confession didn't shake Amy's plans, but rather the weight of the trial began to twist her arms. Out of curiosity, I looked at my watch, barely an hour had passed since the trial of the century.

chapters.title: Chapter Thirty-Four
paragraphs: Several people were smoking in front of the building. I stared at the billowing smoke as it ran towards the sky in the summer heat. I just snagged a few pieces of them with my nose, but even those few puffs had such a strong effect on me as if I were a smoker again, even though it had been many years since I quit. I pondered my morning restlessness. I had been perplexed for a day since I saw that boy in the pictures in the newspaper. Who could he be?

In the courtroom, Amy had heard who knows how many witnesses from both sides. Several girls came forward to testify about their experiences in the darker Neon Nights, but as if they just wanted to bide their time, none of them could say anything new. Neither of them had seen Mortenstein face to face, so it was difficult to connect him to the place they were talking about. What a sophisticated system they have built... I morphed. I wanted to help Amy somehow, and I knew I had the key in my hand, even if I didn't know what kind of lock it opened yet.
"Matt!" I shouted. He came out of the courthouse just at that moment. "You have to help" I waved to him, almost begging, but I was a little lacking in specifics.
Matt was open to me, I showed him the pictures I took yesterday and asked him to say anything that could explain the boy I thought might be important.
"So it's all just a feeling?" he asked, dislodging the fragile pillars of my theory in seconds.
"I would rather call it intuition" I answered. "I can't put it into words, but I'm very uneasy about it. I know it means something, and the more I think about it, the more I feel it is important."
"It can be easy. Just look at the picture. Everyone is there with their children. This little guy is approx. twelve years old. It must belong to someone."
"To Mortenstein?" I asked excitedly.
"That seems logical if he stands next to him," he replied.
"Does Mortenstein have children?" I was surprised.
"There isn't."
"I know that too. But he could be his nephew."
"Does this matter?" Matt asked, getting to the point. "If I were you, I would continue on this path. If he says it's important, then it's worth putting time into it."
"It sure is" I answered. "When is the break?"
"Maybe in ten minutes. Would you like anything until then?" he inquired.
"I don't know. I'll figure it out. I'd rather go back to Amy. If I think of something, I'll let you know."

Not that I had any right to command a detective, but Matt and Wilbur were slowly becoming a part of my everyday life. I hoped that a divine spark would soon arrive and everything that had been in darkness until then would be illuminated.
(Amanda Evans)

The trial progressed, even if terrible fatigue began to plague me after a few hours. Anton seemed very excited during the break, but he didn't say anything specific, except that it was important and not. He said he prefers to keep his nonsense to himself. Regardless, he still approached Matt and had a brief discussion with him about something. I knew he was investigating, I couldn't get him to wean me off this, I thought, I'll talk to him at home about what he was up to today.

Anyway, I had another problem. After listening to the girls, a wave of doubt hit me. I was almost ashamed of what I thought. I was scared of him. What if I can't prove the president had anything to do with Neon Nights. Not to the shop window, which according to them the whole upper class knew about, but to ours, which was the reality for us.

None of us saw the president there but Jess, and I couldn't be sure that his testimony alone would be enough to prove it. Even though everyone knew who Edgar Mortenstein was, the defense cleverly twisted things to make the whole thing look like a misuse of the president's name. They didn't empathize with the girls' suffering, they didn't want to minimize the meanness, they simply pretended that Mortenstein had nothing to do with it all.

Jessica's death was no accident. I just had to connect all the clues together. I was sure that if I succeeded, the picture put together would be strong enough to put the president behind bars, yet I danced with the evidence on a razor's edge.

As much as I wanted to push the thought away, the fact that only Jess had the key to the truth stirred something in me that I had never felt before. I began to doubt that he was telling the truth. Bullshit! I was tired, maybe that's why the thought came to me, but I couldn't help but think about this possibility. What if he lied all along? After all, she never talked about Jake. Not even once. And when she got together with Jeff, she hid everything I should have known about him, and then continued to lie even when the investigation was well underway. I knew he was threatened, but did Jake really write that letter? And why didn't he ever talk about Bill the lawyer? So many questions lay unanswered in front of me.
After the break, the hearing of Timothy Jones followed. The little guy with the cape sat on the witness stand excitedly, yet with a palpable affront.
"You Mr. Jones is the LC. Editor-in-Chief of Rumors?"
"Yes, I am" he answered.
"How long have you been running the paper?"
"Since its inception. from 2000."
"How would you describe LC. Rumors' profile and role in the current press?"

"We are basically a tabloid. But in the highest possible quality. Many people look down on the boulevard, even though it is an important area, especially in today's world. People have always been curious about what is happening in the world above them, which they cannot otherwise see. The world of stars has occupied people since the press was created."
Jones's speech clearly revealed his sociological sensibility regarding the functioning of society.
"Do I understand correctly that the boulevard is not just a job for you?"
"I'm used to saying that the boulevard is my life, although this may seem ridiculous in the eyes of many. It's okay, I've already accepted that they look down on my work."
"What do you think is most important in the boulevard?"

"Definitely the rumours. Did you know that most of the rumors are true? I'm not saying they're all true, but some of them are. And if someone comes across as many rumors in the course of their work as I do, after a while they will see the trends and the true structure of the tabloid world. All I mean by that is that I have it all in my little finger, so if I haven't heard of something, it doesn't exist."
"With that, he already hinted at why we called him here" I explained the reasons for Timothy Jones' presence.
"Yes, well the Neon Nights article, surely."
Suddenly, it was as if the roles were reversed and the witness started asking questions. It was a smiling situation, Jones really got into it.
"A typical case of making people believe of something that it exists, whereas in reality it doesn't."
"Are you saying Neon Nights didn't exist?"
"There might have been something with that name, but not in the form it was in that article."
"I'd like you to explain exactly which article you are speaking of."
"About the issue of July 8, 2010 and the article that I should have rushed into in the afternoon so that I could take it out after sending it to the printer."
"Could you tell me how the incident happened?"

"In the afternoon I received a call from a woman named Jane Smith. Signed in on behalf of the President's Office. He asked me to publish the article in the newspaper that he was going to send soon. At first, I objected that I could not include any articles in that day's issue, since it was completely full. The newspaper has a precise structure, it is easy to follow, which I am particularly proud of."
"And what happened after that?" I inquired.

"The woman kept insisting, she even threatened me so that I would be aware that you can't say no to them, so I went along with it. He sent the article, I took out another one, and finally that day's issue was ready. Then around midnight, when I was already sitting in the car in the parking garage, he called me again to say that there was no way the article would be published, that I should take action immediately. I hesitated again, but quickly realized that it was unnecessary. I called the printer, replaced it with an advertisement and the matter was resolved. It really bothered me, but I tried to forget it as soon as possible. It was an unpleasant, bad feeling. Never before or since has anyone forced me to put something in my sheet with a mandatory argument."
"How did they threaten you?" I asked.
"It doesn't matter, I don't really remember it. It wasn't even that important."
"And what was the article about?"

"It's all bullshit. Basically nothing. That's why I brought up that what I don't know about probably doesn't exist. They wrote about a ball that was attended by the top ten thousand in order to make deals with each other. The event was compared to the balls of the 1700s, and it was written that it was the vision of President Edgar Mortenstein that the social elite would once again organize themselves at events like the evenings of the time. I treated the content of the article with reservations, because I had not even heard of anything like it before, and if the social elite of Love City had really participated in the event, the news would have definitely reached me. I've been trying to find out more about him for weeks, to no avail. It became certain to me that this ball never existed. At least not in the form in which it was discussed."
"And what was the name of this evening?"
"I would rather not say anything about it" Jones replied. "Neon Nights. How can such an event be called that?"
"Do you have any idea why it was necessary for the article to be published in LC. Rumors?"

"I didn't understand it then, and I don't understand it now. I would think of it as propaganda, but I have no idea what the fuss was about. Not least because if I had known about it, I would have volunteered to cover the event myself."

Timothy Jones talked a lot. Incomprehension and offense were felt in his testimony. A small part of him, perhaps to this day, thought he missed out on one of Love City's biggest social events, which understandably hurt him.
One thing was certain. The name Neon Nights came up again and again in different contexts and this fact could not be ignored.

"Dear Court!" I continued. "We followed the contents of the mentioned article. We have come to the conclusion that there is nothing else to report on the event presented above. On the contrary, we found many letters that referred to Neon Nights as a model trainer. This inconsistency allows the assumption that the events and organizations associated with Neon Nights are actually different manifestations of this name, which were connected to the same circle, Edgar Mortenstein's circle."
"Thank you, prosecutor!" answered the judge, then turned to the lawyer. "Does the defense want to question the witness?"
"No, Your Honor! We don't want to deal with articles about Neon Nights."
"It's okay. I'll end the session then" said the judge. "The trial will resume tomorrow at 10 a.m."

chapters.title: Chapter Thirty-Five
paragraphs: Evening of July 21, 2022
I knew that Anton was limping in something all day, so when we got home, I wanted to ask him the question right away, but he got ahead of me.
"I found something yesterday" he said. "Photos from the 2008 elections."
"And what was on them?" I inquired.
"At the time of the election victory, a little boy flanged on the platform. It belonged to someone, but we don't know who."
"What is this plural?"
"I also showed Matt the pictures."
"Was that the nonsense you were talking about during the day?" I asked.
"Ez."
"And why are these pictures so interesting?"
Anton took out his phone and showed them.
"do you see In the first one, he is standing in the front row next to Mortenstein, then in the other pictures he is further and further back, finally disappearing on the edge."
"Nice curly kid," I noted.
"The" answered Anton, and then we sat facing each other in silence for a minute.
"Amy, you noticed too, didn't you?"
"Is it that there are too many curly haired people in this case? I was just wondering how you came up with that" I answered. "How did you come up with this?"
"Intuition."
"So that's why you talked to Matt."
"Yes. He is on to finding out."
"When will he be done with it?"
"Tomorrow during the day."
"Then let's hope so, because I feel like today didn't go very well."
I had been waiting all day for us to talk about the trial. I was hoping Anton would reassure me.
"There isn't enough evidence," I began.
"Of course there is," Anton insisted. "The flash drive is full of it."

"And I don't even have access to half of it. Besides, it doesn't matter what's on it. It's obvious that there were several different Neon Nights. And the President is only linked to the place by Jess's testimony, which won't be enough. They planned it well. They haven't denied anything, so it's up to me to prove beyond a doubt that Mortenstein was the leader. But how, when no one ever saw him?"
We fell silent again. I was exhausted, and I had a gloomy outlook on tomorrow.
"I thought I was doing well with the Neon Nights case at least," I complained. "Instead, now it looks like someone simply misused the President's brand. As if anyone else could have known that name."

"But that's just it, Amy!" Anton said, latching onto a sliver of hope. "What are the chances that Neon Nights would just cross someone's mind? And the President's worldview can be seen in everything. Everything associated with this name stands out from the crowd. If you're a model? Be the best. If you're hosting a ball? Do it with style," then he paused for a moment. "If you want to fuck..."
"Then fuck without limits..." I finished his sentence. I knew exactly what he was talking about.

He was right. At the same time, I also knew how much pressure there is on the court in a case against a president. They cannot convict based on assumptions. Even if the picture comes together for everyone, how can we prove that he was the head of Neon Nights? No one but Jess ever saw him there. And Jessica's testimony, detailed though it was, is useless if no one else can support her most important claims.

"Don't forget about Jake either," Anton spoke up. "You can prove that he was a Neon Nights man, and only a blind man couldn't see that he's connected to the President. The house of cards collapses once you knock out one card. Start with the weakest, Jake!"

Toby McRae arrived at court in his police uniform. He had been a member of the force for eight years, yet he still seemed nervous. His testimony could help establish a connection between Ross Wilson and the hitman who had targeted Anton, and his information could also link Wilson to the Neon Nights. These were all crucial pieces of the puzzle.
"Do you recognize who is in the picture?" I asked McRae.
"Ross Wilson," he answered.
"When did you first meet?"
"Probably January 1st, 2014. That was when I joined the force."
"How was your relationship with the detective?"
"At first we had no relationship whatsoever. We didn't talk."
"Did this change over time?"
"We had to exchange a few words regarding some cases."
"What were these cases?" I inquired.

"Ironically, the first such case was the Neon Nights. We received a call that a girl had died; Wilson took the case immediately and told me to come along. Under the regulations, an officer can never go to a crime scene alone."
"So, if I understand correctly, you ended up there by accident?"
"Actually, yes."
"Did you notice anything unusual about the case?" I prying.

"Several things, yes. Right from the start. I found it unusual that Wilson threw himself into the case right away, because normally after an emergency call, patrol officers go to the scene first, and they notify the detectives. In this instance, however, the call came directly from the club."
"So, if I understand correctly, they called Wilson specifically?"
"Actually, yes," replied Toby McRae.
"Did you report this to anyone?"
"I had only been there a few weeks. Nothing good could have come of reporting Detective Wilson."
"What did you witness at the club?"
"When we got there, Wilson went in alone. I waited in the car. After a few minutes, two patrol officers left the Neon Nights."
"So they must have been dispatched there via the emergency line," I supplemented the testimony.
"Yes, in all probability."
"Why do you think the club called Wilson directly when they had already summoned the police through the emergency line?"
"I can only assume that one person called Wilson and someone else called the police."
"What happened next?"
"After ten minutes, Wilson came out and we headed back to the station. In the car, I asked him what had happened. He said one of the girls had died in the bathroom. He suspected an overdose."
"Did you believe him?"
"I had no reason not to believe him, but I found it strange that the matter was just left at that."
"Do you know the girl's name?" I inquired.

"Yes, Katherine Mayers. Wilson compiled a very brief report about her, in which he surprisingly wrote that the girl had been shot in the head. He had told me in the car it was an overdose. He was obviously trying to mislead me."
"How long were you colleagues with Wilson?"

"He left the force in 2015. Ostensibly, he went to the Bahamas because he came into a large sum of money. Even then, I thought he might have taken a bribe, specifically because of cases like the Mayers affair."
"This year, however, thanks to you, we discovered he returned."

"After I was questioned about Wilson, I started investigating him myself. I found out that he had been to Love City several times since then, the last time obviously when we found his body in the hotel room in the Nouveau Palais."
"Has it since been revealed who killed him?"

"Not really," McRae replied. "But we found a few numbers in his phone, including the number of the hitman who had attacked you a few days earlier. We managed to trace the calls, and they had indeed spoken to each other."
"So it's fair to say that Ross Wilson instructed the hitman to kill us?"
"All signs point to that, Prosecutor Evans."
"Did you find anything else related to him?"
"Yes. A few days before his death, cell tower data placed him in the Liberty district, close to the area where Jake Cooper lived."
"Close to it, or exactly there?"

"We're talking about cell tower information, so we only know he connected to the transmitter that broadcasts in that area. But another interesting detail came to light. On the morning of the day Jessica Marsh was killed, the same data shows he was in Montaukville."
"So right around the time the Black Mustang crashed into another car, as Jefferson Morris testified?" I inquired.
"Yes, exactly then."
"And was he still there in the evening when the assassination took place?"
"No," the patrolman replied. "Ross Wilson was already back in Love City by then."

"Let's summarize, Mr. McRae," I took the initiative. "Do you think it's possible that Ross Wilson was a Neon Nights operative used to cover up sensitive cases for the organization, and that this connection was maintained even after Wilson's Bahamian detour?"
"Yes, I believe Wilson was working for the Neon Nights, and had a hand in closing numerous cases prematurely. In addition, it appears he went to work again in Love City before his death."
"Thank you, Patrolman McRae!"

Mortenstein sat through the entire testimony with a frozen smile on his face. That face irritated me. It was smug and overconfident. I didn't believe this act for a second. I was sure he was eating himself up inside. It had to be so, even if he truly believed he would get away with it. He had no reason to hope that after the trial he would be the same president he was before. After fourteen years in power, a case like this tarnishes a man's reputation even if he eventually leaves the courtroom victorious, I thought. Yet his smile was directed at me, and its message was: you can't catch me!
The President's attorney asked Patrolman McRae only a few questions.
"When you and Ross Wilson arrived at the Neon Nights, did you see the President there?"
Toby naturally answered no, since if he had seen him, he would have mentioned it much earlier.
"During your investigation of Ross Wilson, did you find any lead whatsoever to suggest that President Edgar Mortenstein was connected to the Neon Nights club?"
"I did not find anything of the sort, counselor," he replied briefly.
"I see. The defense has no further questions for the witness!"
